faqs.question: How much should I expect to pay an IGCSE home tutor in LA Mer?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai market rates put an in-home one-to-one visit at roughly AED 180 to AED 500 an hour including travel, with Bestimate's rate table giving 180 to 350 and independent home tutors quoting 200 to 500. The same qualified tutor working online sits in a AED 150 to AED 300 band, and specialist exam-year support runs AED 200 to AED 450 or more. Those are market figures from sources read in October 2026, not IB Gram prices. For a Jumeirah 1 address, a meaningful share of the in-home premium is the evening drive rather than the teaching.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to a LA Mer apartment?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; home tutoring is a service we run only in India. Lessons for LA Mer families are delivered one-to-one over live video, scheduled in Gulf Standard Time, with a shared whiteboard both tutor and student can write on. We target the home-tutor search because that is the phrase parents type, and we answer it honestly rather than implying a car will arrive. The trade is a tutor chosen for your child's syllabus instead of one chosen for living within a drivable radius of the beachfront.

faqs.question: Is paying more per hour actually worth it for Year 11?
faqs.answer: For an exam-year student, usually yes, but not for the reason families expect. The gain is not a better personality or more homework help; it is someone who has worked the specific paper your child sits and knows where its marks hide. Twenty-one hours with a specialist at AED 280 commonly moves a grade that thirty-three hours with a generalist at AED 180 does not, despite costing the same. For Years 7 to 9 the inversion runs the other way and a lower tier is genuinely sufficient, which is the cheapest time to buy support.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE series does a LA Mer student sit, and does the March window apply?
faqs.answer: Cambridge International runs IGCSE and O Level exams in a June series and a November series, and UAE candidates sit those two. The February and March series is offered to India only, so any advice pointing a Dubai family at a March window is wrong for this country. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states it is essential to use the correct timetable version for your zone, so confirm both series and zone with your school's exams officer.

faqs.question: Do private tutors in the UAE need a permit, and does it cost them anything?
faqs.answer: They need one, and it is free. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed individuals, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone quoting you a permit fee is describing something that does not exist. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule has been published, so no amount should be quoted to you.

faqs.question: What is the difference in cost between Core and Extended support?
faqs.answer: Very little per hour, and a great deal in total. The hourly market rate barely moves between tiers, but Extended covers more content and is examined on harder papers, so it needs more hours across the year. The expensive error is the other way round: paying specialist rates to chase a grade 7 while a child sits Cambridge 0580 Core, which caps at grade 5. Ask the school which tier your child is entered for before you buy anything. That one question has saved families an entire term's spend.

faqs.question: Where exactly does a paid tutor have to stop on an IGCSE coursework component?
faqs.answer: Yes, within a clear boundary. A tutor may teach the skills the component assesses, explain the criteria, read a draft the student has written and say where it misses the criterion, model technique on a different example, and coach planning around the deadline. A tutor may not write, complete or rewrite any part of work that must be the student's own. One site competing for this search sells completed Internal Assessments; that is malpractice and the consequence falls on the student. IB Gram tutors teach, review and give feedback only.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week do LA Mer families usually start with?
faqs.answer: One session a week per subject is the common starting point, moving to two in the eight to twelve weeks before a series. Families who start at three or four sessions a week across several subjects almost always overspend, because at that volume tutoring stops supplementing school and starts duplicating it. We also suggest a review at six sessions: enough to see whether a named failure mode has closed, not enough to have committed a term's budget to a plan that is not working.

faqs.question: Are Arabic and Islamic Education counted towards UAE equivalency?
faqs.answer: No. For the British track, Ministry of Education equivalency requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at no less than grade E or grade 3, and Arabic and Islamic education are not included among those five. A ranking UAE tutoring site states six subjects are needed; the sourced requirement is five. Students must also show one accredited subject at Advanced Level at grade E or better, or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Verify current requirements with the Ministry rather than relying on any tutoring page, including this one.

faqs.question: What time can lessons start after the school run from Al Safa?
faqs.answer: Pickup for the schools most LA Mer secondary students attend runs between about 2:40pm and 3:30pm, so a 4pm or 4:30pm online session is realistic on a weekday and a 6pm one is comfortable. That earlier window is one of the practical differences from a home visit, where the tutor's own drive across Dubai usually pushes the earliest slot to 6pm. Families with children at different schools often stagger two one-to-one sessions across the same evening, which is straightforward online and difficult with a visiting tutor.

faqs.question: Do you teach both Cambridge and Pearson Edexcel IGCSE?
faqs.answer: Yes, and the distinction matters more than parents expect. Cambridge uses four-digit syllabus codes such as 0580 Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry and 0610 Biology, with Core and Extended tiering in several subjects. Pearson uses codes such as 4MA1 and 4PH1 and structures some qualifications differently. A tutor who teaches one board and assumes the other will prepare your child for a paper they are not sitting. Ask your school which board each subject is entered with; it is not always the same board across subjects.

faqs.question: Who regulates the school my child attends in Jumeirah?
faqs.answer: Dubai private schools are regulated by KHDA, the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain fall under ADEK, Sharjah under the Sharjah Private Education Authority, Ras Al Khaimah under its Department of Knowledge, and Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah under the federal Ministry of Education. IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation or partnership from KHDA or any other regulator, and names them here only to explain who does what.

faqs.question: Is there any discount for tutoring two children in the same household?
faqs.answer: Household arrangements are discussed at the consultation rather than priced on a page, because the honest answer depends on whether the two children need the same subject at the same level. Two siblings in Year 10 taking Cambridge 0580 can sometimes share a session productively. A Year 8 student and a Year 11 Extended candidate cannot, and putting them together saves money while wasting both hours. Online scheduling does make back-to-back one-to-one slots on the same evening straightforward, which is usually the more useful economy.

faqs.question: What happens if no specialist tutor is free for the subject we need?
faqs.answer: We tell you, which no competitor page in the researched set does. For a niche subject or an unusual hour, a UAE-based specialist may genuinely not be available, and the options are a realistic match time, a tutor in another time zone whose working hours still land in a Gulf Standard Time evening, or a recommendation to wait. What we will not do is put a generalist into a specialist slot and let you discover the gap in March. That substitution is how a family loses both the money and the term.

faqs.question: Should we wait for school mocks before booking a tutor?
faqs.answer: Usually no, because mocks arrive too late to be a starting gun. The most productive tutoring block runs eight to twelve weeks before the mock window, so the mock measures a student who has already fixed something rather than confirming a problem everybody knew about. If the mocks have already happened, the marked paper becomes the most valuable document you own: bring it, and the first session can be diagnosis-free and get straight to the two or three topics that are costing marks.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-la-mer.closingHeading: What to do next if you are pricing IGCSE support in LA Mer
dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-la-mer.closingBody: Find the most recent marked paper, check with the school which board, syllabus code and tier your child is entered for, and confirm whether they are sitting the June or the November series. Those three facts turn a vague search for an IGCSE home tutor in LA Mer into a specific request a specialist can answer. Then take the free trial lesson, one per family and before any payment, and watch whether the tutor asks about the tier before teaching. If they do not, keep looking. If no specialist is free at your hour, we will say so rather than filling the slot.

intro.heading: What a Living Legends family actually gets for the money
paragraphs: Two tutors quoting AED 250 an hour can be selling quite different products, and the number hides the difference entirely. One marks a past paper between sessions and arrives with a diagnosis. The other arrives and asks what the student would like to look at. The second is cheaper to deliver and costs the same, and in a market where three of the six most visible pages publish no price at all, a parent has very little to compare against.

Living Legends adds a second layer that applies to any visiting service. It is a gated community of villas and apartment towers off Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road, between Dubai Sports City, Motor City and Remraam, with no secondary school inside the gates. A tutor coming in has to be registered or met, has to park, and has to get here through evening traffic on an arterial road. When the booked hour starts at six and the tutor reaches the door at ten past, the family has bought sixty minutes and received fifty. Twice a week across a school year, that is a measurable quantity of teaching paid for and not delivered.

The third layer is information, and it is free. International GCSE is awarded by both Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel, with codes such as Cambridge 0580 and Pearson 4MA1 for mathematics, and Cambridge tiers several subjects into Core and Extended while Pearson tiers mathematics into Foundation and Higher. A Cambridge Core entry cannot exceed grade C. If a family is paying for months of tuition against a ceiling that already sits below the grade they need, the hourly rate is irrelevant: the purchase is worth nothing.

Put those three together and a useful rule emerges. Spend money on information first, diagnosis second and hours third. The information costs one email to the school's examinations officer asking for the board, the syllabus code and the tier. The diagnosis costs three to five sessions and produces a written gap list. Only then do hours convert reliably into marks, and only then is comparing two quotes a sensible exercise.

IB Gram's own position is stated rather than implied. Lessons run one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time, so nothing in the price pays for a journey and nothing is lost at a gate. Home visits are a service we operate only in India; nobody is sent to a Living Legends address. The trial lesson is a full session, free, with no card and nothing to cancel, and it is used as a diagnostic rather than a sales meeting. A parent should finish it knowing which gap is costing marks and roughly how many sessions closing it would take. Everything below is the detail needed to interrogate any quote, including ours.

Consolidating topics while they are taught costs less than rebuilding them a year later, and the qualified band of AED 150 to 300 an hour does the most work per dirham. A diagnostic against the real syllabus code early in Year 10 prevents the most expensive error available.
programmes.countryNote: Students from this community travel out for secondary school, so Year 10 sessions have to be sized for a school night after a long journey. Short frequent slots at a mid rate outperform long weekend sessions at a premium rate while content is still being taught.

programmes.name: Year 11 and the series
programmes.description: The expensive year and the one where specialist rates are justified, because the work becomes board-specific technique rather than content. Bestimate puts specialist examination-year support at AED 1,000 to 2,000 and upward per month for a weekly session, and frequency usually rises above weekly in the final weeks.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge candidates in the UAE sit June and November, and Pearson Edexcel runs May/June and November. A November resit is a genuine second chance, but results reach students in January, so the financial decision about an August-to-November intensive is taken before the information arrives.

programmes.name: Post-16 and equivalency
programmes.description: A Levels or the IB Diploma, with options constrained by International GCSE tier and grade. For Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, five accredited subjects at no less than E or grade 3 are required, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level.
programmes.countryNote: Getting the five-subject count right in Year 9 costs nothing. One ranking competitor page states six subjects, which is incorrect, and a family who built an option block from that page has made an expensive mistake at no charge to anybody but themselves.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-living-legends.subjectsIntro: Different subjects convert hours into marks at different rates, mostly because specialist supply and the amount of technique involved vary. These notes are about where a budget goes furthest.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: The best-supplied subject, so rates sit mid-band rather than at a scarcity premium. Hours convert efficiently because the main failure is method presentation rather than understanding, and that is a habit with a defined number of sessions attached.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Fewer specialists, so expect the upper half of the qualified band. Electricity and forces are taught early and compound, which means money spent in Year 10 goes considerably further than the same money in the spring of Year 11.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Difficulty concentrates in moles, electrolysis and organic chemistry, which makes short targeted blocks unusually cost-effective. A diagnostic that locates the block is worth more than a term of general revision.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The subject where families most often buy too many hours, because the content volume makes coverage feel necessary. Marks are lost in answer structure on long questions, so a few sessions on technique beat extended content work.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences
subjects.description: Content is reduced across all three sciences, and the classic overspend is buying separate-science support and paying for removed topics. Confirming the award before booking saves weeks of fees for the price of one email.

subjects.name: English as a First Language
subjects.description: Well supplied and mid-band. Progress depends on repeated marked writing, so the real cost driver is how much the tutor reads between sessions. Ask what marking is included before comparing two quotes.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language
subjects.description: A separate specification with its own components. Families who book first-language support for a second-language entry pay for material of limited use, which is among the cheapest errors to avoid and the most common to make.

subjects.name: Business Studies and Economics
subjects.description: Application and evaluation carry the top band, not definitions. Hours spent on definitions are close to wasted, so a tutor who opens with past-paper evaluation questions is spending the budget correctly.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Thinner specialist supply and higher rates. The expensive mistake is booking support for one when the student is entered for the other, since the two specifications share almost nothing in content.

subjects.name: Arabic
subjects.description: Compulsory in Dubai private schools, with separate classes required for Arab and non-Arab students. Support works from the school's own material, since for mandatory subjects any additional content needs prior Ministry of Education permission.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-living-legends.regionsIntro: Where a family lives changes what a visiting tutor charges and what reaches the student. These notes are about the cost consequences around Living Legends.

regions.name: Living Legends
regions.note: Gated, compact and off an arterial road, with no secondary school inside. Visiting quotes carry a full travel premium and lose minutes at the gate, which is why the online comparison band is the relevant one here.

regions.name: Dubai Sports City
regions.note: The nearest dense cluster, where visiting tutors price more competitively. Academy training occupies the early evening for many households, and a weekend visit commands the top of the in-home band.

regions.name: Motor City
regions.note: The closest neighbourhood with a real independent tutor market, a short drive north. Even there the Diploma and Extended-tier specialists are few, because scarcity at that level is city-wide.

regions.name: Remraam and Mudon
regions.note: Residential communities to the south with provision for younger years. Short distances, awkward timing, and approach roads that congest at the same hour as the school run.

regions.name: Al Barsha South and Dubai Hills Estate
regions.note: Where many secondary students from this community attend school. Twenty to thirty minutes out depending on the hour, which is the reason an early-evening visit is unrealistic and expensive.

regions.name: Arabian Ranches
regions.note: Established villa communities to the west with a wider tutor market and IB provision. Still a meaningful drive from the Living Legends gate at the hour families want a session.

schoolClusters.city: Nearby provision for the earlier years
schoolClusters.note: Schools in Motor City, Sports City and Remraam serve most primary and middle-years children from this community. KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that Dubai private school fees would not increase for the following academic year, which makes tuition the variable line in a household education budget.

schoolClusters.note: International GCSE teaching for this community sits further out, along the Al Khail Road corridor and in the Al Barsha and Jumeirah area. Seven new private schools and 16,846 places are being added across the emirate in the next intake, four of them British curriculum.

sections.heading: Itemise the hour before comparing two quotes
paragraphs: The hourly rate is the least informative number in a tutoring quote, and asking better questions costs nothing. What a parent should want is the itemised version: what happens inside the session, what happens outside it, and what happens when something goes wrong. Two providers at the same rate routinely differ on all three.

Start with the session itself. Is it sixty minutes of teaching or fifty-five with setup? Are the materials written for the student's actual syllabus code, or generic worksheets that would suit either board? Is the lesson structured against the school's scheme of work, or against the tutor's preferred order? Each of those changes what the hour produces, and none of them appears in a price.

Then the work outside the session, which is where good tutors spend unpaid time. Is written work marked between sessions, and how much? Is there a short written note to the parent, and does anyone compare progress against a starting diagnostic? Does the tutor read a returned school assessment before the next session, or arrive cold? A rate that includes marking and a rate that does not are different products at the same number.

Finally the terms. What is the cancellation window, what happens to a missed session, does a package expire, and is VAT inside the figure? We do not state the UAE VAT treatment of tuition as a general fact, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority citation and a tutoring page is the wrong source for a tax position. What any provider can tell you is whether their own quoted figure is inclusive, and a provider who cannot answer clearly has told you something useful.

sections.heading: The sourced rate card, read from the top down
paragraphs: Most pages that publish rates at all start at the cheap end, which flatters the budget band. Reading from the top down is more instructive, because it shows what the extra money is for and where it stops buying anything.

At the top, premium named or examiner-led provision reaches AED 500 to 650 and upward, with BartyED advertising AED 650. That band is buying reputation and, sometimes, claimed examiner status. Treat the second with care: no tutor should be described as an IB or Cambridge examiner without evidence of current status, and any suggestion that examiner status grants access to marking, boundaries or paper content should end the conversation. Below that, IB, International GCSE and A Level specialists run AED 200 to 450 and upward, with TutorChase at AED 270 and Bestimate putting examination-year specialist support at AED 200 to 450 plus. That band is buying board-specific technique, and for a Year 11 Extended paper it is the honest answer.

In the middle, qualified online subject tutors sit at AED 150 to 300, with Unitors publishing International GCSE from AED 150 and IB from AED 200. That band is buying somebody who knows the specification and will mark work. At the bottom, budget online provision runs AED 45 to 150, with EdFlik from AED 45 to 65 and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52. That band is buying frequency and patience, which for Years 7 to 9 is often exactly right.

Sitting across all of it is the in-home band at AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel, with Bestimate at 180 to 350 and independent home tutors reaching 500. It is not a quality tier. It is a delivery tier, and what it buys is a journey. In a gated community off an arterial road it also costs minutes at the gate, so it is the one band where the parent pays more and receives less teaching per hour. IB Gram does not sell UAE home visits at all; the service exists only in India.

sections.heading: The hidden costs of a visiting tutor in a gated community
paragraphs: This is the part of the in-home proposition that nobody prices, and in Living Legends it is not trivial. A visiting tutor has to clear a gate. That means being pre-registered by the household, or met, or waiting while security confirms the visit. Then parking. Then finding the villa or the tower entrance, which in a community arranged around a golf course is not always obvious to somebody arriving for the first time.

The direct cost is teaching minutes. A booked hour that starts ten minutes late is a sixty-minute fee for fifty minutes of work. At two sessions a week across roughly thirty-six school weeks, consistent ten-minute losses amount to twelve hours of tuition paid for and not received, which at the in-home band of AED 180 to 500 is a serious sum. Most families never calculate it because it arrives in small pieces.

The indirect costs are reliability and scope. A tutor delayed on Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road at twenty past six has effectively cancelled half a session, and that happens often enough to wear an arrangement out by the second term. Meanwhile, the pool of tutors willing to make this journey twice a week at the hour everybody wants is small, so the family chooses from fewer people and the ones who do come price the uncertainty into the fee.

Set against that, in-home has a genuine case for some students. A child under roughly Year 5, or a student with significant attention difficulties, benefits from physical presence in a way that is hard to replicate on a screen. That is worth paying a premium for. A Year 10 or 11 student working through past papers on a laptop is not in that category, and for them the premium is pure logistics.

sections.heading: The free information that changes the value of every hour
paragraphs: One email to the school's examinations officer is the highest-return action available to a family in this community, and it costs nothing. Ask for the board, the syllabus code and the tier for each subject, and ask whether the entry is final. Those four answers determine whether any subsequent spending works.

Cambridge International and Pearson Edexcel both award International GCSE. Cambridge uses codes such as 0580 Mathematics, 0625 Physics, 0620 Chemistry and 0610 Biology, with Core and Extended tiers in several subjects; Pearson uses 4MA1, 4PH1, 4CH1 and 4BI1 among others, with Foundation and Higher tiers in mathematics. Exactly one syllabus code appears across the whole competing area-page cluster researched for this project, which says how rarely this is asked.

The tier is the expensive part. A Cambridge Core entry leads to grades C to G and an Extended entry to A* to E, with the tier set at entry by the school on internal evidence. Once entries close, no amount of tutoring changes the ceiling. A household paying AED 600 to 1,200 a month in a subject where the ceiling sits below the grade they need has bought nothing of use, and this is the single largest waste this market produces.

There is a second lever worth asking about. Pearson offers a modular route in some subjects, where units can be sat across more than one series with the better result carried forward, which splits one high-stakes moment into two. Whether a centre enters modularly is a centre decision rather than a published default, so it has to be asked. Both questions, the tier and the modular option, belong in the same email.

sections.heading: Where the money goes wrong in a community like this
paragraphs: The waste patterns are consistent, and all of them are avoidable with information a parent already has or can get free. None is about being charged too much per hour.

The first is paying the in-home premium for a student who works perfectly well on a screen, which in a gated community means paying for a journey and losing minutes at the gate on top. The second is buying volume at the budget band for an examination-year paper, where the work is board-specific technique and the cheap tutor is reconstructing the specification from memory. Twenty hours at AED 60 moves fewer marks than six at AED 270 in that situation.

The third is spending against a capped tier, already described, and it is the most expensive of all. The fourth is buying support for the wrong specification: first-language English material for a second-language entry, Computer Science for an ICT candidate, separate-science revision for a coordinated or combined award. Each of those costs a term of fees and produces revision that does not match the paper.

The fifth is subtler and very common in households with more than one child. Spreading a fixed budget evenly across four subjects and two children for a whole year, so that nothing receives enough attention to move. Concentrating the same money on a diagnostic across everything and then one or two blocks where the marks are actually going produces more, and it leaves a record of what changed.

sections.heading: Group classes, tuition centres and the per-student illusion
paragraphs: A group class looks like simple arithmetic: divide the tutor's rate by four and the price per student falls. For breadth that arithmetic holds. For the problem most families in this community are trying to solve, it does not.

A group moves at the group's pace. If four Year 11 students share a class and each is losing marks in a different place, the hour addresses at most one of them while the others sit through content they already have. Group teaching is efficient at delivering a syllabus and inefficient at closing a specific deficit, which is what examination-year tutoring exists to do. Used earlier, in Years 8 and 9, a group class covering ground is often good value and a reasonable way to keep costs down.

Tuition centres with premises in Dubai are a different commercial and legal animal from an individual tutor. A centre requires a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, with initial approval first, a maximum of six months to complete the permit and licence steps, and annual renewal requested at least thirty days before expiry. That permit is worth asking about, and it also explains why the phrase approved is used loosely in this market: the permit belongs to the institution, not to a person, and it says nothing about teaching quality.

IB Gram operates no centre, office or branch in the UAE, and holds no KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, Ministry, Cambridge or Pearson approval or accreditation. We explain what each body does and link to it. A provider claiming an approval it cannot evidence has told a parent something useful about the reliability of its other claims, prices included.

sections.heading: Budgeting across two years, and what a resit adds
paragraphs: Families want a total rather than a rate, and the honest way to build one is to multiply a monthly band by the months, then price the examination-year intensity separately because frequency rises at the end. Bestimate's Dubai monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session give the base: AED 240 to 600 budget, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range, AED 1,000 to 2,000 and upward for specialist examination-year support.

A two-subject plan running from the start of Year 10 to the June series is roughly eighteen school months. At the mid band that is a substantial commitment, and it is worth asking whether both subjects need the whole period. Often they do not: one may need a diagnostic and a ten-week block in Year 10, with the budget concentrated on the second subject in Year 11. Spreading an identical sum evenly across both for eighteen months is the default and rarely the best use of it.

A resit changes the arithmetic in a specific way. Cambridge runs June and November series in the UAE, and Pearson Edexcel runs May/June and November; the February and March series is India-only. The catch is timing. Pearson's November 2026 International GCSE final timetable ran to 19 November 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, so a November candidate waits roughly nine weeks and learns the outcome in January, after many sixth-form conversations have begun. An August-to-November intensive is therefore money committed before the information arrives, and it should be discussed with the school first.

One further item that families forget to budget: entry as a private candidate carries a fee set by the centre rather than by the board, and it varies. Ask the centre directly rather than relying on any figure quoted on a tutoring page, including this one. And note that KHDA confirmed in May 2026 that private school fees in Dubai would not rise for the following academic year, which makes tuition the variable line in a household education budget and worth deciding deliberately rather than letting it accumulate.

sections.heading: What money cannot buy at any band
paragraphs: A page about cost should be explicit about where spending stops working, because the alternative is implying that money and outcome are the same variable. They are not.

No provider can promise a grade. Not at AED 50 an hour and not at AED 650. Grades depend on the work a student does between sessions, on what a particular series asks, and on where boundaries fall, and nobody selling tuition controls any of those. We publish no grade promise, no improvement promise and no refund tied to an outcome. We also publish no satisfaction or results figure, because a statistic without the number of students, the date and the method behind it is not evidence, and most such figures displayed in this market carry none of the three.

Money cannot reopen a closed entry, cannot substitute for the student doing problems themselves, and cannot buy board material. Cambridge and Pearson past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade boundary tables are their copyright, and unreleased material carries a malpractice exposure as well. A provider advertising a download library has an unresolved problem a family using it would be sharing. Nor may a tutor produce assessed work: where coursework exists, a tutor teaches, questions and gives feedback on what the student wrote, and the student signs the authentication declaration.

Finally, tutoring is not required for anything regulatory. Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track asks for five accredited International GCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level. Checking that on moe.gov.ae costs nothing. Equivalency is not a service IB Gram performs, expedites or guarantees, and any page implying that paying for tuition affects a regulatory process is manufacturing pressure.

process.title: Concentrate the budget, then review

whyPoints.title: No travel and no gate in the price
whyPoints.description: Lessons run over live video, so nothing in the fee pays for a journey and no minutes are lost at security. In a gated community off an arterial road that is the largest avoidable cost a family faces, and most households never add it up.

whyPoints.description: Each AED band here names who published it and when it was gathered. Three of the six most visible pages competing for these searches publish no price at all, and one asks the price question in its own FAQ list before declining to answer it.

whyPoints.title: The hour itemised before it is sold
whyPoints.description: Teaching minutes, materials written for the right syllabus code, marking between sessions and written parent reporting are stated rather than assumed. Two quotes at the same rate are frequently different products, and the difference lives in that list.

whyPoints.title: The tier checked before the invoice
whyPoints.description: A Cambridge Core entry caps the grade at C and no spend changes that once entries close. If the ceiling sits below the grade a family needs, we say so and provide a written diagnostic for the school instead of billing monthly against it.

whyPoints.title: The free trial is genuinely free
whyPoints.description: A full session, no card, no condition and nothing to cancel. Where a condition applies to anything described as free, it belongs on the same screen as the word, because an unstated condition there is a consumer-protection problem as well as a trust one.

faqs.question: What does an IGCSE home tutor charge to come to Living Legends?
faqs.answer: The Dubai market quotes in-home one-to-one tuition at AED 180 to 500 an hour with travel included, with Bestimate at 180 to 350 and independent home tutors reaching 500. In a gated community off Sheikh Mohammed Bin Zayed Road expect the upper half of that band, because the tutor is pricing the journey and the uncertainty. IB Gram does not sell UAE home visits at all; that service exists only in India. Our lessons run one-to-one over live video, which places the comparison in the AED 150 to 300 qualified online band instead.

faqs.question: How much teaching time does a gated community actually cost us?
faqs.answer: More than most families calculate. A visiting tutor has to be registered or met at the gate, park, and find the villa or tower entrance, and then has to arrive through evening traffic on an arterial road. A booked hour that starts ten minutes late is a sixty-minute fee for fifty minutes of work. At two sessions a week across roughly thirty-six school weeks, consistent ten-minute losses come to about twelve hours of tuition paid for and not received, which at in-home rates is a serious figure.

faqs.question: Two Living Legends quotes match on rate. What separates them?
faqs.answer: Ask for the itemised version. Is the hour sixty minutes of teaching or fifty-five with setup? Are materials written for the student's actual syllabus code or generic? Is written work marked between sessions, and how much? Is there a short written note to the parent? What is the cancellation window, do unused sessions expire, and is VAT inside the figure? Two providers at the same number routinely differ on every one of those, and the difference is the entire product rather than a detail.

faqs.question: Should we pay specialist rates for Year 10, or wait until Year 11?
faqs.answer: For most subjects, the qualified band of AED 150 to 300 an hour is the right level in Year 10, with the specialist band of AED 200 to 450 reserved for the examination year. Year 10 work is consolidation while content is being taught, which is the cheapest form of tutoring per mark because nothing has to be rebuilt. Year 11 work is board-specific technique, and that genuinely requires somebody who has worked the specification and its markschemes. Spending in the wrong direction at either end is the commonest overspend in this market.

faqs.question: Is the tutor's permit something we pay for?
faqs.answer: No. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years, with MoHRE's own service page listing no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private-sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. Anyone tutoring without it is subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no amounts are published. A licensing line item in a quote is charging for something free.

faqs.question: How much does the exam board tier affect what we should spend?
faqs.answer: Completely, in one case. A Cambridge Core entry leads to grades C to G while an Extended entry reaches A* to E, and the tier is set at entry by the school. If the grade a family needs sits above the Core ceiling, monthly spending against it buys nothing once entries close. The only intervention that works is a short diagnostic against the real specification, written up and taken to the school before the deadline. After that date the money is better redirected to another subject entirely.

faqs.question: Are group classes cheaper in a useful way?
faqs.answer: For breadth, yes; for a specific gap, rarely. A group moves at the group's pace, so if four students are each losing marks somewhere different, the hour addresses at most one of them. Group teaching delivers a syllabus efficiently and closes a deficit inefficiently, which is what examination-year work is for. In Years 8 and 9 a group class covering ground can be sound value. Centres running them in Dubai need a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute, which is worth asking about.

faqs.question: What is the single most expensive mistake families here make?
faqs.answer: Paying an in-home premium for a Year 10 or 11 student who works perfectly well on a screen, and then losing minutes at the gate on every visit. The premium over a qualified online tutor is AED 30 to 200 an hour before any lost time, and the teaching inside the hour is not better for having arrived by car. The genuine exception is a child under roughly Year 5 or a student with significant attention difficulties, for whom physical presence does real work and is worth paying for.

faqs.question: How should we budget from Year 10 to the June series?
faqs.answer: Multiply a monthly band by the months and price the final stretch separately. Bestimate's Dubai estimates give AED 240 to 600 a month for budget provision, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-range and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and upward for specialist examination-year support, each for a weekly session. Eighteen school months across two subjects at the mid band is a substantial sum, and it is usually better spent as a diagnostic plus concentrated blocks than as an even monthly retainer in every subject at once.

faqs.question: Does a November resit cost more than it returns?
faqs.answer: That depends on the timing more than the teaching. Cambridge runs June and November series in the UAE and Pearson Edexcel runs May/June and November; the February and March series is India-only. The complication is the wait: Pearson's November 2026 timetable ran to 19 November 2026 and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026, so the outcome arrives in January, after many sixth-form conversations begin. An August-to-November intensive is money committed before the information arrives, so discuss conditional arrangements with the school first.

faqs.question: Is VAT inside the tuition figure we are quoted here?
faqs.answer: Ask, and get it in writing. We do not state the UAE VAT treatment of tuition as a general fact, because that requires a Federal Tax Authority citation and a tutoring page is the wrong place to take a tax position. What any provider can and should tell you is whether the figure they quoted you is inclusive or exclusive, and whether they hold a tax registration number. A provider who cannot answer either question clearly has told you something useful about how they invoice.

faqs.question: Will anybody refund us if the grade does not improve?
faqs.answer: No reputable provider should offer that, and we do not. A refund tied to an outcome is a promise with no mechanism behind it, because grades depend on the work a student does between sessions, on what a particular series asks and on where boundaries fall. What we do offer is a free full-length trial lesson with no card, a per-session arrangement rather than a locked package, and a written diagnostic you can measure progress against. Those protect a family's money in a way an outcome promise cannot.

faqs.question: Are past papers included in what we pay for?
faqs.answer: Not reproduced from the boards, no. Cambridge and Pearson past papers, mark schemes, syllabus documents and grade boundary tables are their copyright, and unreleased material carries a malpractice exposure as well. A tutor cites the official source, works from material the school has legitimately issued, and writes equivalent practice questions in the same style and at the same difficulty. A provider advertising a paper library is offering you a copyright problem rather than an advantage, and it should raise a question about their other claims.

faqs.question: Can we concentrate spending on one child and one subject?
faqs.answer: Usually that is the better plan. Spreading a fixed budget evenly across four subjects and two children for a year means nothing receives enough attention to move, and families end up with a year of fees and no clear change. A diagnostic across everything, followed by one or two funded blocks where the marks are actually going, costs less and leaves a record of what changed. Online delivery also makes consecutive slots for two children cost nothing extra, because no second journey is being paid for.

intro.heading: Meydan has no school inside it, and that shapes everything
paragraphs: Meydan sits around the racecourse inside Mohammed Bin Rashid City, built out quickly with villas, low-rise and Meydan One, and almost no schools within its own boundaries. Every school-age child in the district travels out. That single fact decides more about a tutoring arrangement here than curriculum, board or budget, and it is the thing nobody writes about.

Where they travel to is a short list. Hartland International School and North London Collegiate School Dubai are in Sobha Hartland, a few minutes away inside the same wider development. Kings' School Nad Al Sheba, Repton School Dubai and GEMS Modern Academy are across in Nad Al Sheba. Further out are Safa Community School in Al Quoz, Swiss International Scientific School Dubai at Al Jaddaf, and the Al Barsha and Silicon Oasis schools for families who chose on provision rather than proximity.

Each of those produces a different arrival time at home. A Sobha Hartland family can be back and settled before 15:30. A Nad Al Sheba family lands around 16:00. An Al Quoz or Al Barsha family is closer to 16:45, later if there was an activity. And a child in Year 11 at any of them may have a school revision session, a sports fixture or a club that moves the whole thing by an hour on two days of the week. A weekly tutoring slot that ignores all of that is a slot that will be rescheduled four times and then abandoned.

Dubai held 387,441 private-school students across 227 schools in 2024-25, with UK-curriculum schools accounting for 37% of enrolment, the largest single share across seventeen licensed curricula. Most of those schools run IGCSE at sixteen before splitting students towards A Level or the IB Diploma, which makes Year 11 in this corridor a year with two exits and a very full week.

IB Gram delivers tuition to UAE families as one-to-one lessons over live video, timed to Gulf Standard Time. We do not send tutors to addresses anywhere in the UAE — home visits are a service we run only in India. On a school-run page the reason is concrete rather than philosophical: a tutor driving into Meydan at 15:30 is driving against the traffic every family in the district is sitting in, and the twenty minutes District One's internal roads absorb before a car reaches Al Khail belongs to somebody's invoice. Online, a 16:00 session starts at 16:00.

One thing worth collecting before any first conversation, and it is not the subject. Find the school's fixture and club calendar for the term, and work out which single weekday afternoon has nothing recurring on it. That afternoon is the only slot that will still exist in March, and every other decision about IGCSE support in this district is downstream of it. Families who skip that step book a session on a Tuesday, discover a fortnightly fixture, move it twice, and stop by half term having paid for four lessons and learnt nothing about where the marks were going.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-meydan.programmesIntro: The school run changes shape at each stage of a British-curriculum education, and the stage decides which slots are available. These are the four stages a Meydan family passes through, described by what the week actually looks like at each.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3
programmes.description: The lightest week of the four and the easiest to schedule into. Days typically end earlier than in the senior years, homework load is moderate, and after-school activities are the main competitor for an afternoon. This is the stage at which a weekly slot is most likely to survive a full term unchanged, which makes it the cheapest time to fix a subject gap.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai, Key Stage 3 runs alongside KHDA's mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies lessons, required in all private schools regardless of the licensed curriculum. For Meydan families new to the emirate — and the district has a high share of them — Arabic from a standing start is the most common first request at this stage.

programmes.name: IGCSE Year 10
programmes.description: The week tightens. Nine or ten examined subjects begin properly, coursework starts in the subjects that carry it, and sports and arts commitments are usually at their peak before exam year pulls them back. A weekly slot still works, but it needs to sit on a day with no fixture, and the right day is identified from the activity calendar rather than guessed.
programmes.countryNote: Year 10 is also where the tier decisions in tiered subjects become visible, and where a timed higher-tier past paper gives the only real evidence for the entry conversation in the autumn of Year 11. Meydan families arriving mid-Year 10 from another system frequently need a syllabus audit before anything else.

programmes.name: IGCSE Year 11
programmes.description: The fullest week in the British curriculum. School revision sessions appear at short notice, mock series dominate the spring term, coursework deadlines land, and the final weeks before the series need two or three tutoring sessions a week rather than one. Scheduling becomes the limiting factor on what support is even possible.
programmes.countryNote: Across the Meydan corridor Year 11 also carries the post-sixteen decision, because several nearby schools offer both A Level and the IB Diploma. Families who know by the January mocks which exit they are leaning towards can target the remaining months; those who decide in July are choosing from a narrower set.

programmes.name: What follows Year 11
programmes.description: A Level or the IB Diploma, both of which reshape the week again: fewer subjects, longer independent study periods, and in the Diploma's case three internal assessments plus the Extended Essay and Theory of Knowledge. Evening slots become more viable because the student is older, and the scheduling problem eases just as the workload grows.
programmes.countryNote: For universities inside the UAE there is a separate Ministry of Education equivalency step. The British-track rule is five accredited GCSE or IGCSE subjects at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, excluding Arabic and Islamic education, plus one Advanced Level subject at E or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade. Verify current requirements on moe.gov.ae.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-meydan.subjectsIntro: Subject choice interacts with the timetable, because some IGCSE subjects need a long uninterrupted session and others do not. Below are the subjects Meydan students ask for, each with a note on the session shape it actually wants.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: Needs concentration rather than length, so an alert 45 minutes at 16:00 outperforms a tired 90 at 19:00. Cambridge sets a non-calculator paper at both tiers and Pearson does not, which is the first thing to establish. Practice must be on the student's own tier or it demoralises or under-stretches.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Pearson 4PH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
subjects.description: The most mathematical of the three sciences and the one where tiredness shows first, because a rearrangement abandoned halfway loses the back half of a question. Best placed early in the week and early in the afternoon. Graph work and gradients are the reliable marks.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620, Pearson 4CH1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
subjects.description: Suits shorter, more frequent sessions than physics, because the losses are precision habits — state symbols, ionic equations, trends described rather than explained — and habits respond to repetition rather than to long blocks. A 45-minute slot twice a week beats 90 minutes once.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610, Pearson 4BI1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or single tier
subjects.description: Content-dense and command-term sensitive, which makes it the subject most workable in a later or tireder slot, because recall and answer structure survive fatigue better than calculation does. Useful to place on the day with a fixture before it.

subjects.name: English as a First Language (Cambridge 0500)
subjects.description: Needs a longer session than the sciences, because a timed writing task cannot be split sensibly. This is the subject most often worth a weekend block rather than a weekday slot for Meydan students whose school day ends late.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510, 0511)
subjects.description: Four skills including speaking and listening, which makes it the one subject where a shorter weekday slot genuinely works for all components. The summary task carries concentrated marks and is a drillable technique rather than a language ability.

subjects.name: Business Studies (Cambridge 0450)
subjects.description: Case-study driven, so sessions need enough length to read a stimulus and write a judgement from it. Calculation questions on break-even and cash flow are reliable marks and routinely skipped under time pressure, which makes them a good target for a short session.

subjects.name: Economics (Cambridge 0455)
subjects.description: Diagrams are assessed rather than decorative, so a short block on diagram discipline — labelled axes, shifted curves, new equilibrium marked — buys marks across every paper and fits a 45-minute weekday slot comfortably.

subjects.name: Computer Science (Cambridge 0478)
subjects.description: Pseudocode is marked to the syllabus conventions, which catches fluent coders who translate loosely, and trace tables are high-value and low-glamour. Both are mechanical and suited to short frequent sessions rather than long ones.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.levels: Extended or Higher tier students only
subjects.description: Taken alongside the main qualification by students heading for A Level Mathematics or Higher Level IB maths. Timetabled thinly in most schools, which is exactly why it is the subject most often supported outside school in this corridor.

subjects.name: Arabic as a first or additional language
subjects.description: KHDA requires Arabic in all Dubai private schools regardless of curriculum, with separate classes organised for Arab and non-Arab students. Support works within the school's own approved material, because KHDA prohibits different or additional content for mandatory subjects without Ministry permission.

subjects.name: Geography (Cambridge 0460)
subjects.description: The skills paper is where a prepared student gains most — map reading, graph interpretation, data response — and all of it is practisable in a few short sessions. Extended answers need named located examples, which is recall and survives a later slot.

sections.heading: Which schools Meydan feeds, and what each does to the afternoon
paragraphs: A tutoring slot in this district is set by the school, not by the house. Meydan children travel to four distinct clusters, and the difference between the closest and the furthest is more than an hour of usable afternoon across a week. Anybody planning support without that information is planning for an average student who does not exist.

The table below sets out the clusters and what each does to the arrival time. The end-of-day bands are deliberately given as ranges rather than exact times, because schools differ by year group, by day of the week and by term, and a page that printed a precise finishing time for a named school would be wrong somewhere within a month. Confirm your own child's with the school; what the table is for is the shape.

The pattern that matters is this. Families whose school sits inside Sobha Hartland have the easiest week in the corridor and can use 15:30. Families travelling to Nad Al Sheba land around 16:00, which still works. Families travelling to Al Quoz, Al Barsha or Silicon Oasis are home late enough that a weekday session is a compromise, and the honest advice for them is usually one weekend block rather than two tired weekday slots.

There is a second-order effect worth naming. The further the school, the more likely the child is in a bus or a long car journey, which means homework starts later and the evening compresses from both ends. For a Year 11 student that compression is why tutoring in this corridor so often ends up on a Friday or a Saturday — not because weekends are better in principle, but because the weekdays have already been spent.

sections.heading: The four o'clock problem
paragraphs: There is a narrow window in a Dubai school day when a teenager can still learn something demanding, and in Meydan it is shorter than most families realise. School ends mid-afternoon, the journey home eats thirty to seventy minutes depending on the cluster, and concentration starts falling away by early evening. Everything useful has to happen inside that gap or be moved to a weekend.

This is where a visiting tutor's arithmetic becomes a problem rather than an inconvenience. A tutor driving into Meydan for 16:00 is travelling at exactly the hour that every school in the surrounding communities is emptying, in the opposite direction to the families they serve. District One's internal roads and limited exits onto Al Khail absorb around twenty minutes before a car reaches a main road. The result is familiar to anybody who has tried it: a 16:00 slot that begins at 16:40 and finishes when the student has already stopped absorbing anything.

Online delivery removes the travel on one side only, which is the side that can actually be removed. The child still has to get home; the tutor does not have to arrive. That turns a theoretical 16:00 slot into an actual one, and it means a missed or delayed school bus shifts the session by fifteen minutes rather than cancelling it.

The practical consequence for planning is that session length should follow arrival time rather than subject preference. A student home at 16:00 can do a full hour of maths. A student home at 16:45 should do 45 minutes, and the subject chosen for that slot should be one that survives a shorter session — biology or geography recall rather than physics calculation. Matching the subject to the slot rather than the slot to the subject is the whole trick.

sections.heading: A real Year 11 week in Meydan
paragraphs: Abstract advice about study schedules founders on the fact that a Year 11 week is already full. School revision sessions appear at short notice in the spring term. Sports fixtures take one or two afternoons. There is an Arabic, Islamic Education or Social Studies commitment inside the school week under KHDA requirements. Coursework deadlines arrive in clusters. A tutoring slot has to fit into what is left, and what is left is usually two weekday afternoons and part of a weekend.

The table below is a worked example rather than a prescription, built for a student travelling to Nad Al Sheba and home around 16:00. It shows the thing most plans leave out: which days are already gone, and therefore which two are worth defending. The exercise of filling it in honestly, with the school's actual fixture calendar beside it, takes twenty minutes and prevents three months of rescheduling.

Two rules make it work. First, pick the day with nothing recurring on it and protect that slot absolutely, including from the family's own social calendar. Second, accept that one subject gets the good slot and the others get maintenance, which means deciding which subject that is rather than rotating by guilt. A student doing twenty minutes of recall in two subjects and a full session in the third will outperform one doing three half-sessions.

The mock season breaks the pattern deliberately and should. For six weeks around the mocks and again in the final run before the series, the cadence rises to two or three sessions a week in one subject, and other commitments give way. That is the point at which a visiting-tutor arrangement in this district stops being practical, because three journeys a week through pick-up traffic is a different proposition from one.

sections.heading: Ramadan, and a school day that moves
paragraphs: Ramadan reorganises a Meydan week more thoroughly than any other factor, and a tutoring plan that treats it as a disruption rather than a phase will lose a month. School hours shorten. The family day reorganises around Iftar and later sleep. Energy in the late afternoon is lower, and for fasting students a 17:00 session is not the same session it was in February.

The approach that survives is to decide the Ramadan pattern in advance rather than improvising it. Sessions generally move either earlier, into the gap created by the shorter school day, or later to post-Iftar timing, and the productive length drops in both cases. A focused 45 minutes is worth more than a tired 90, and the subject placed in that slot should be the one that survives a shorter session.

For Year 11 students sitting the summer series, the cadence usually holds and the clock changes. A four-week gap in the spring is expensive in June, so pausing entirely is rarely the right call for an exam-year student, while shortening and moving sessions almost always is. For Year 10 and Key Stage 3 students a genuine pause is more defensible, and saying so is more useful than selling continuity nobody needs.

The other fixed feature of a Dubai school week, year round, is the mandatory-subject requirement. KHDA requires Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral Studies in all private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, with instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit and schools advised that any mandatory-subject lesson runs at least 25 minutes. Those minutes sit inside the school day rather than outside it, so an IGCSE revision plan competes with them rather than borrowing from them.

sections.heading: The home-tutoring question, and arrival time
paragraphs: A home tutor in Meydan is a reasonable thing to want and the market supplies it. The honest account of what it gives and what it costs belongs on a page like this, because the trade-off here is unusually tilted by geography rather than by anything abstract.

What it gives is presence: a parent can see the session, a fifteen-year-old cannot drift to another tab, and a tutor in the room notices a wandering attention sooner. Those matter, particularly in Year 10. What it costs in this district is time. There are no schools inside Meydan, so a visiting tutor travels into the district at precisely the hour the surrounding school runs are emptying, and the internal road network adds its own twenty minutes. The market also prices the journey: in-home one-to-one runs AED 180 to 500 an hour including travel against AED 150 to 300 for a qualified subject tutor online, figures read in October 2026.

The arithmetic gets worse exactly when it matters. One visit a week is manageable. The mock aftermath and the final six to eight weeks need two or three sessions a week, which is two or three journeys, two or three travel premiums, and a fixed slot that cannot move when the school adds a revision class on Thursday. That is the point at which in-home arrangements in this corridor tend to collapse, and it is the point at which the student needs them most.

IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; that service exists only in India. The table below is therefore reasoning behind an existing decision rather than a pitch, and it is written so a Meydan parent can check it against their own week. The number that actually lands on a card is monthly, and it changes three times during Year 11 as the cadence changes rather than as the rate does. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 in the middle, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 or more for specialist exam-year support. Packages published in the market include around AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home visits.

For a Meydan family the scheduling point and the cost point are the same point. A weekend block is one session rather than two, which makes it cheaper as well as more realistic for families on the long school run. Two short weekday sessions cost more than one long one and are usually worth it in chemistry and maths, where habits respond to repetition. Three sessions a week is an exam-term cadence and should be budgeted as a six-to-eight-week spike rather than a standing rate.

Three questions separate providers in this market more reliably than the headline rate: the session length behind the quoted figure, whether VAT is included, and who bears a session missed because a school bus was late. sections.heading: Year 10 and Year 11 need different slots
paragraphs: The same family, the same house and the same school produce two different scheduling problems a year apart, and most tutoring arrangements are set up in Year 10 and never revisited. That is why so many of them are being rescheduled weekly by the spring of Year 11.

Year 10 has the better week. Sports and arts commitments are usually at their peak, which takes afternoons, but there are no school revision sessions, no mock series dominating a term and no cluster of coursework deadlines. A single protected weekday slot works, and it is the cheapest point at which to rebuild genuinely missing content, because nothing is urgent and the hours are unhurried.

Year 11 reverses that. Activities often reduce, which frees afternoons, but school revision sessions appear at short notice, the mock series takes a term, coursework lands, and the final weeks need two or three sessions a week. The arrangement that has to change is the standing single slot: it is no longer enough in the spring and it was more than necessary in the autumn. Planning the step up in advance is better than discovering it in February.

There is also a tier and exit decision sitting inside that year. The tier entry decision in tiered subjects closes in the autumn of Year 11 at the school's entry deadline, and the evidence for it is a timed higher-tier past paper sat in Year 10 and marked against the official scheme. The post-sixteen choice between A Level and the IB Diploma, available at several schools in this corridor, is best leaned towards by the January mocks. Both are calendar decisions, which is another reason a Meydan plan should be dated rather than open-ended.

Year 11: activities reduce, school revision sessions and mocks arrive
Plan the step up to two or three sessions a week before February
The tier entry decision closes at the school's autumn deadline
Lean towards the A Level or Diploma exit by the January mocks

sections.heading: Mock season, and the fortnight with a shelf life
paragraphs: The mock series is the most informative thing that happens in Year 11, and in this corridor it is also the point at which a tutoring arrangement either earns its fee or quietly stops being worth it. The information has a short shelf life: the fortnight after results is when a mock script is worth something, because that is when the student still remembers what they were thinking.

The work is unglamorous. Get the script back from the school, not just the grade. Go through it mark by mark and sort every lost mark into one of four categories: content not known, command term misread, arithmetic or notation slip, or ran out of time. Tally the categories across all subjects. One almost always dominates, and in this corridor it is usually timing in maths and the sciences and command terms in the humanities.

Then act on the dominant category only, for a fixed period, and leave the others alone deliberately. A student whose losses are mostly timing does not need more content; they need twenty timed sections and a rule about when to abandon a question. A student whose losses are content needs a written list of what is being abandoned, because with four months left they cannot cover everything and spreading effort evenly is the same as choosing at random.

This is also the point where the slot has to change, and where a Meydan family on the long school run usually moves to a weekend double plus one weekday session rather than trying to fit three weekday slots into a week that does not have them. Papers come from the school's licensed access or the board's own platform; we do not host, reproduce or distribute board papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables or subject guides.
bullets: Request the script, not only the grade
Sort every lost mark: content, command term, slip, timing
Work the dominant category for a fixed fortnight
Write down the topics being abandoned and show the student
Move to a weekend double plus one weekday slot if the run is long

sections.heading: Weekend blocks, and when they beat weekdays
paragraphs: Weekend tutoring has a slightly apologetic reputation, as though it were what families settle for when the week fails. For a significant share of Meydan students it is simply the better arrangement, and saying so is more useful than pretending every child can learn algebra at 17:30 after a forty-minute bus ride.

Weekends win in three specific cases. First, the long school run: a family travelling to Al Barsha, Dubai Hills or Silicon Oasis is home late enough that weekday sessions are a compromise in both attention and length. Second, subjects that cannot be split — a timed English writing task, a full past-paper section, a coursework draft read properly — which need an uninterrupted stretch that a weekday evening rarely offers. Third, mock season, when a weekend double plus one weekday slot is often the only way to reach three sessions in a week that already has school revision classes in it.

Weekdays win when the subject wants repetition rather than length. Chemistry precision habits, maths non-calculator fluency, trace tables in computer science: all of those respond better to two short sessions than one long one, and in the Sobha Hartland and Nad Al Sheba clusters two short weekday slots are genuinely available. Matching the pattern to the subject is worth more than arguing about which is better in principle.

One practical note on weekends that applies to any format. A weekend session that follows a late Friday night and precedes a family lunch is not a long session, it is a short session with a long slot around it. Pick a start time the student can actually meet, keep it the same every week so it becomes a habit rather than a negotiation, and treat the first fifteen minutes as warm-up rather than as teaching.

sections.heading: Before you book: permits, quotes and the bus
paragraphs: Three checks before paying anybody, and all three matter more in a commuter district than they would elsewhere. None takes long and all three are the kind of thing that gets discovered at the wrong moment.

The first is the permit. Private tutoring in the UAE runs on one: the MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, and u.ae states it is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page is 'Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing', listing no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Anyone calling it costly or optional is misinformed, and u.ae states that those tutoring without one are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws — with no published fine schedule, so no figure should be quoted to you.

The second is the quote. Session length behind the hourly figure, whether VAT is included, whether materials are charged separately, and what happens to unused sessions if you stop. Four short answers, in writing, before the first payment rather than after a disagreement.

The third is specific to Meydan: who bears a session missed because the school bus was late or a fixture overran. In a district where every child commutes, it will happen, and the answer should be agreed in advance rather than negotiated at the time. A provider with a clear answer has thought about families like yours. Separately, IB Gram holds no approval, accreditation, licence or partnership from KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoHRE, the Ministry of Education, Cambridge or Pearson, and claims none; where a provider claims a regulator has approved its tutors, ask for the permit number.
