programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: Two-year courses assessed by terminal written papers in the June and November series, with most subjects tiered Core or Extended and the sciences adding either a practical test or an alternative-to-practical paper. Every centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and Cambridge states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam otherwise.
programmes.countryNote: Cambridge also runs Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests at other points in the year, which occasionally confuses families about when the real series falls. For a Year 11 in Nad Al Sheba the dates that matter are the June series and, as the resit route, November.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Available in May-June and November each year, with Foundation and Higher tiers. The November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series.
programmes.countryNote: Those published dates are the most useful planning anchors available to a Dubai family, because they show how the year actually falls: results in late August for a summer series and in January for a November one. Always open the live official timetable rather than relying on a restated date, including the ones here.

programmes.name: International A Level
programmes.description: The usual post-16 continuation for a Dubai IGCSE student who does not move to the IB Diploma. Entry depends on IGCSE tier and grade, which is why a results-day conversation is often also a sixth-form conversation.
programmes.countryNote: Ministry of Education British-track equivalency requires one accredited Advanced Level subject at no less than grade E, or two Advanced Subsidiary subjects at the same grade, alongside five GCSE or IGCSE subjects at no less than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education excluded from that count.

programmes.name: IB Middle Years Programme
programmes.description: The IB route at the same ages, assessed against four criteria per subject group rather than by terminal papers, with no external series unless the school offers eAssessment.
programmes.countryNote: Relevant in this cluster because Nad Al Sheba has both IB continuum schools and a British school within a short radius, so households here sometimes run one child on an external examination calendar and another on continuous criterion assessment. The two need completely different scheduling.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-nad-al-sheba.subjectsIntro: What each subject needs depends on the point in the year as much as on the syllabus. These notes name the code and say when in the calendar that subject is best worked on.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580)
subjects.description: Fluency work belongs in the autumn and cannot be built in a final term. Technique work, legible method and timed question sets, belongs in the last ten weeks. A tier review belongs in Year 10, before entries close, because Core cannot be awarded above grade C.

subjects.name: Mathematics A (Pearson 4MA1)
subjects.description: Two calculator-permitted papers, Foundation to grade 5 and Higher to grade 9. The calendar point is the same: build fluency early, drill papers late, and settle the tier while the school can still act on it.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625)
subjects.description: Circuit analysis and graph technique respond well to late work because they are skills rather than content. The alternative-to-practical paper is the ideal final-term target, since it rewards method and can be drilled from past papers entirely.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620)
subjects.description: Moles work must be secure before the final term; it is foundational and cannot be rebuilt in eight weeks. Organic nomenclature and qualitative analysis answers, by contrast, are late-term wins because they are pattern recognition.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610)
subjects.description: The one subject where late work genuinely pays, because the terminology load rewards spaced retrieval and the application technique is teachable quickly. Two shorter sessions a week beat one long one in a revision phase.

subjects.name: Coordinated and Combined Sciences (0654, 0653)
subjects.description: Revision must be organised by paper rather than by science, which matters most in the final term when students drift towards whichever science they find easiest and arrive with one third of the content thin.

subjects.name: English as a First Language (0500)
subjects.description: Directed writing improves inside eight weeks; reading response improves more slowly. In a final term, prioritise the writing paper and the technique for approaching an unseen passage rather than attempting to broaden reading experience.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (0510, 0511)
subjects.description: Listening and reading tasks drill well late. The tier decision, which affects both the grade ceiling and the vocabulary expectation, belongs much earlier and is frequently left too late to change.

subjects.name: Economics and Business Studies (0455, 0450)
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy and case application are among the fastest late-term gains in the whole timetable, because the marks are lost to a habit rather than to missing knowledge. Four to six sessions can move these noticeably.

subjects.name: History and Geography (0470, 0460)
subjects.description: Source handling and structured answers drill well in a final term; content breadth does not. The honest advice eight weeks out is to secure the answer structure on the topics already known rather than attempt the ones that were missed.

sections.heading: Where you are in the year, and what support should be doing
paragraphs: The single most useful question to answer before engaging anybody is which part of the calendar you are in, because it changes the product rather than the intensity. An autumn enquiry is a content enquiry: the school is still teaching syllabus, gaps are small, and a weekly hour at the qualified band of roughly AED 150 to 300 does useful work without urgency. A final-term enquiry is a technique enquiry, and the same hourly rate buys something completely different.

The transition between the two is the mock block, and it is where most families get the timing wrong in both directions. They either cancel tutoring during mock weeks because the fortnight is busy, losing the most informative hour of the year, or they wait until after mocks to engage anybody at all, arriving with a stack of marked papers and ten weeks left. Either way the diagnosis that the mocks produced goes unused.

After the series there is a fourth phase that is rarely planned at all: results and what follows. Published Pearson dates give the shape. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026; November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. A family receiving a disappointing result in late August has days to decide about a resit and roughly eight to ten weeks to prepare for a November sitting.

Mapping those four phases onto your own child is a ten-minute exercise and it changes what you should buy. The table below sets out what each phase needs and, just as importantly, what it does not. Buying content teaching eight weeks out is the commonest and most expensive mismatch in this market, and it happens because the family is anxious and the provider is selling hours rather than asking what the date is.

sections.heading: The eight weeks before a series, week by week
paragraphs: Eight weeks is the window most families actually engage in, so it deserves a concrete plan rather than general encouragement. The principle throughout is that the student does the work between sessions and the session is spent on the gap between what they wrote and what the scheme rewarded. That inverts the usual arrangement, where a tutor talks for an hour, and it is why fewer sessions move the same distance.

The first two weeks establish the baseline. The student sits one past paper per subject under real timed conditions with no notes, self-marks against the scheme, and records not only the errors but the marks the scheme rewarded that they did not provide. Those two documents per subject are the plan. Without them, the following six weeks are guesswork dressed up as revision.

Weeks three to six are the repair, question type by question type. Not topic by topic: at this stage the useful unit is the kind of question, because a student who cannot handle a six-mark explain question is losing those marks everywhere regardless of topic. Each session takes one question type, works it against the scheme, and sets more of the same for the week. Two shorter sessions a week beat one long one for retention in this phase.

Weeks seven and eight are full papers under timed conditions, which belong at weekends because they cannot be sat properly on a school night at 17:30. The final session is logistics and calm: confirming the correct zone timetable with the examinations officer, checking equipment and calculator settings, and agreeing that the arrangement ends at the first paper. Tutoring that continues through the series itself usually displaces sleep rather than adding marks.

sections.heading: Mock results: the fortnight that decides the revision plan
paragraphs: A marked mock paper is the most information a family will ever get about an IGCSE candidate before the real thing, and most of it is thrown away. The student looks at the grade, feels bad or relieved, and the script goes into a bag. The marks were there, annotated, question by question, showing exactly which question types failed and where time ran out, and nobody read them.

Reading them properly takes an hour per subject and produces something no amount of general revision can: a ranked list. Which question types lost the most marks. Whether the losses were clustered at the end of the paper, which is a timing problem, or spread evenly, which is a knowledge or technique problem. Whether method marks were forfeited to illegible working. Whether a particular command term was consistently misread.

That is also why cancelling tutoring during the mock fortnight is the costliest scheduling decision available. Families do it because the two weeks are busy, which they are, and because the sessions feel less urgent when the papers have already been sat, which is exactly backwards. The papers have been sat; that is what makes the hour valuable.

A practical note for this cluster. Nad Al Sheba households have short school runs and heavy activity calendars, so the fortnight when mocks return usually collides with a fixture block. The useful compromise is to move the sessions rather than cancel them, which costs nothing when there is no journey attached, and to accept that in a mock fortnight two sessions in one week is better value than one session in each of two weeks.

sections.heading: Results day, remarks and the resit decision
paragraphs: Published dates give the shape of this phase. For the June 2026 series, Pearson results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. For the November 2025 series, results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those are backward-looking citations rather than promises about a future sitting, and Pearson issues provisional timetables ahead of each series, so the live official timetable and your school's examinations officer are the authority for your own dates.

On results day there are three decisions, and they interact. Whether to query a mark, which runs through the school and the board rather than through any tutor, and which has its own deadline set by the board. Whether to resit, and in which subjects. And whether the result changes the post-16 route, because a sixth-form or college place may depend on a specific grade in a specific subject.

The resit decision deserves honesty rather than encouragement. A grade that is sufficient for the intended next step is a finished matter, and spending eight weeks and several thousand dirhams to improve a grade nobody will ask about is a poor use of both. Where a grade genuinely blocks a route, the November series is the realistic second attempt and the window is roughly eight to ten weeks from results.

What that window suits is a finite technique block in one or two subjects. The candidate has already met the syllabus, so the gains come from paper technique, question-type recognition and working legibility rather than from content teaching. Six to ten sessions with an end date at the first paper is the shape. What it does not suit is a rolling arrangement, and a provider who converts a resit into an ongoing monthly commitment has sold you something other than what you came for.

sections.heading: The November route, and the zone timetable Cambridge warns about
paragraphs: UAE candidates sit the June and November series. The February and March series exists but is offered to India only, which is worth stating directly because advice to the contrary circulates widely enough to have misled families. Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in the June and November series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests at other points in the year.

The administrative detail that can genuinely cost a candidate an examination is the zone. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones, states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, and says that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. That is Cambridge's own position, not an interpretation, and it means a timetable downloaded from a general search result is not safe to plan from.

Eliminating that risk takes one email to the examinations officer asking which zone the centre is in and confirming the paper dates and times for each subject entered. For a candidate sitting several subjects it is worth doing in writing and keeping. It costs nothing, and it removes the only part of this process where a family can lose a grade for a purely administrative reason.

Pearson handles timetabling differently but the discipline is the same. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May-June and November, the November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026, and provisional timetables are published well ahead of each series. The habit to build is opening the live official timetable rather than trusting a restated date anywhere, this page included.

sections.heading: Fitting a revision calendar around the Dubai year
paragraphs: The UAE academic year contains a period of shortened school hours, during which the whole useful study window shifts to after Iftar, and it can fall inside a revision phase. A fixed in-home arrangement handles this badly, because a tutor whose availability depends on a drive across the city at a particular hour either renegotiates or disappears. An online arrangement moves a 17:30 slot to 21:00 for the period and moves it back afterwards.

For a student in the final run to a series, that shift is often an improvement rather than a problem. The post-Iftar window is quiet, the child is not coming straight off a school day, and longer stretches of concentration are easier to find than they are at 17:30 on an ordinary Tuesday. Full timed papers in particular sit better there than in a weekday evening.

Two other features of the Dubai year interact with a revision plan. The long holiday blocks, during which many families in this cluster travel, which an online arrangement handles by shifting the clock rather than suspending the work. And the school's own internal examination timetable, which compresses a term's assessment into a few weeks and means a student may want three sessions in one week and none in the next.

None of that requires a contractual conversation when there is no journey in the arrangement. It is the single clearest practical advantage of the format in a city with a calendar this variable, and it matters most precisely in the eight weeks when the calendar is least flexible and the stakes are highest.

sections.heading: What eight weeks cannot fix, said plainly
paragraphs: A tier cannot be changed eight weeks out. Cambridge Core candidates cannot be awarded above grade C and Pearson Foundation candidates cannot exceed grade 5, and once entries have closed that ceiling is fixed regardless of how well the candidate performs or how much tutoring is purchased. Anybody implying otherwise in a final-term conversation is misleading a family at the worst possible moment.

Two years of missing content cannot be taught in eight weeks either. Where a candidate has genuine gaps across most of a syllabus, the honest options are to secure the topics they do know well enough to score reliably, to accept the likely grade and plan the post-16 route around it, or to consider the November series as the real target with the summer sitting treated as practice. All three are better than an eight-week attempt to cover everything, which typically produces a candidate who knows a little about all of it and can answer none of it under time pressure.

Nor can fluency be built late. Algebraic automaticity in mathematics, moles arithmetic in chemistry and terminology recall in biology are all products of repetition across months. They can be improved in eight weeks and they cannot be created. This is the strongest argument for buying support in Year 10, and it is only ever made convincingly in retrospect.

What eight weeks genuinely can do is substantial: paper technique, question-type recognition, working legibility that recovers method marks, timing that stops a candidate losing the last fifteen marks of every paper, and the mark-scheme literacy that turns knowledge into marks. For a candidate who knows the content and underperforms on papers, that is often two grades. Being clear about which of those two situations a family is in is the most useful thing a first conversation can produce, and it is free.
bullets: A tier cannot change after entries close; the grade ceiling is fixed

sections.heading: Permits, materials and the claims to refuse in a panic
paragraphs: Families engage tutors fastest when they are worried, which is exactly when the basic checks get skipped. So they are worth stating. Private tutoring in the UAE requires the MoHRE private tuition work permit, introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18 and university students.

MoHRE's service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time, and is applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Individuals offering private tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws; no schedule of amounts has been published, so none appears here. Because the permit is free and fast, asking for it in August is no less reasonable than asking in October.

On materials: Cambridge and Pearson syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables are copyright, and reproducing or distributing them is infringement. We do not supply them. Work from what the school has issued and from the official sources directly. In a final-term panic, a provider offering a large library of other people's assessment material is offering something they do not own, which is a reason for caution rather than relief.

And the claims to refuse. Nobody should describe themselves as approved, accredited or licensed by KHDA, the Ministry of Education, Cambridge or Pearson without a permit number to show; IB Gram holds none and claims none. Nobody should promise a grade or an improvement, because what happens in the examination hall is not a product. And nobody should tell you, eight weeks out, that a Core entry can be lifted above a grade C.

faqs.question: We are eight weeks from the exams. Is it worth hiring an IGCSE tutor now?
faqs.answer: It depends on which problem you have, and an honest provider will tell you which. If your child knows the content and underperforms on papers, eight weeks of timed technique, question-type recognition, working legibility and mark-scheme literacy can be worth two grades. If two years of content are genuinely missing, eight weeks cannot teach it, and the better plan is to secure the topics already known, accept the likely grade, or treat the November series as the real target.

faqs.question: What should tutoring be doing in the autumn term of Year 11?
faqs.answer: Closing content gaps while they are still small and cheap to close. The school is still teaching syllabus, nothing is urgent, and a weekly hour at the qualified band of roughly AED 150 to 300 does genuinely useful work. This is also the last comfortable point to evidence whether a tier is realistic. What autumn should not be spent on is general revision across every subject, which has nothing specific to practise yet.

faqs.question: Should we pause tutoring during the mock exams?
faqs.answer: Keep the slot and change what it does. During the mocks themselves there is little to teach, but the fortnight when marked papers come back is the most valuable tutoring of the entire two-year course: the student has just demonstrated, question by question, exactly where the marks go. An hour per subject reading those scripts against the schemes produces a ranked list of question types. Families cancel that fortnight because it is busy, which is precisely backwards.

faqs.question: How do we read a marked mock paper usefully?
faqs.answer: Look for pattern rather than score. Losses clustered at the end of the paper are a timing problem; losses spread evenly are knowledge or technique. Working an examiner could not follow has forfeited method marks that were genuinely earned. A command term consistently misread shows up across several questions. Group the losses by question type rather than by topic, because a student who cannot handle a six-mark explain question is losing those marks everywhere.

faqs.question: What does the week-by-week plan look like in the final eight weeks?
faqs.answer: Weeks one and two establish a baseline: one timed past paper per subject with no notes, self-marked against the scheme, recording the marks available and not claimed. Weeks three to six fix question types one at a time, mixing in the earlier ones as they hold. Weeks seven and eight are full papers at weekends, because they cannot be sat properly at 17:30 on a school night. The last session is logistics and the arrangement ends at the first paper.

faqs.question: When do IGCSE results reach students in Dubai?
faqs.answer: The published Pearson pattern gives the shape: June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026, and November 2025 results reached students on 22 January 2026. Those are backward-looking citations rather than promises about a future series. Pearson also issues provisional timetables ahead of each sitting. Confirm your own dates with the school's examinations officer and the live official timetable rather than relying on a figure restated anywhere.

faqs.question: Our June result was disappointing. Should we resit in November?
faqs.answer: Only where the grade genuinely blocks the next step. A grade sufficient for the intended sixth form or college place is a finished matter, and spending eight weeks and several thousand dirhams improving a grade nobody will ask about is a poor use of both. Where a route is genuinely blocked, the window from late August to a November sitting is roughly eight to ten weeks, which suits a finite technique block in one or two subjects with an end date at the first paper.

faqs.question: What should a November resit block actually consist of?
faqs.answer: Paper technique rather than content, because the candidate has already met the syllabus. Six to ten sessions: rework the failed papers against the mark scheme, identify the question types that lost the most marks, drill those under timed conditions, then sit two full papers properly marked. Confirm the entry, tier and timetable zone with the examinations officer early. The block should end at the first paper, and a provider converting it into a rolling monthly arrangement has sold you something else.

faqs.question: Which exam series do Dubai students sit, and when?
faqs.answer: The June and November series. Cambridge runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in those two series, with Primary and Lower Secondary Checkpoint tests at other points in the year. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May-June and November; its November 2026 final timetable ran from late October to 19 November 2026. The February and March series exists but is offered to India only, so it does not apply to a UAE candidate however often that advice circulates.

faqs.question: What is the Cambridge zone timetable and why does it matter?
faqs.answer: Cambridge allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones and publishes a separate timetable version for each. It states that it is essential to use the correct version for your zone and that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one. That is Cambridge's own position, which means a timetable found through a general search is not safe to plan from. One email to your examinations officer confirming the zone and the paper times removes the risk.

faqs.question: Can a tier still be changed close to the exams?
faqs.answer: No. Once entries have closed the tier is fixed, and Cambridge Core candidates cannot be awarded above grade C while Pearson Foundation candidates cannot exceed grade 5, regardless of performance or tutoring. Anybody suggesting otherwise in a final-term conversation is misleading a family at the worst moment. The tier conversation belongs in Year 10, where two sessions at ordinary rates can produce evidence a head of department will discuss while there is still time to act.

faqs.question: How does the shortened-hours period in Dubai affect a revision plan?
faqs.answer: It shifts the whole study window to after Iftar, and for a candidate in the final run to a series that is often an improvement. The post-Iftar hours are quiet, the child is not working straight off a school day, and longer stretches of concentration are easier to find than at 17:30 on an ordinary weekday, which makes it a good time for full timed papers. With no journey attached to the arrangement, moving a 17:30 slot to 21:00 for the period is a calendar change and nothing more.

faqs.question: Does a Nad Al Sheba address make a revision timetable easier to hold?
faqs.answer: Yes, with one caveat. Several schools sit inside or beside the community, so runs are short by Dubai standards and children are often home by 15:45, which makes 16:30 workable and two weekday sessions genuinely feasible in a revision phase. The caveat is the activity load: this cluster carries a heavy sport and riding calendar, and in a final term the fixtures usually have to give way to the papers. Agreeing that in advance avoids a weekly argument.

faqs.question: Should sessions continue during the exam series itself?
faqs.answer: Rarely, and only on request between specific papers. Tutoring that runs through the series usually displaces sleep and revision time rather than adding marks, and a candidate sitting several subjects across a few weeks needs recovery more than instruction. Agree in advance that the block ends at the first paper, with the option of one targeted review between two papers if a particular subject genuinely warrants it. intro.heading: The question is not whether they can teach it - it is whether they know which one it is
paragraphs: Parents in Oud Metha asking for an IGCSE home tutor are usually worrying about something more exact than general competence. The worry is this: will whoever we hire actually know the examination my child is sitting, as opposed to a subject with the same name? It is a well-founded concern, and the answer turns on a piece of information most families do not have to hand - the syllabus code.

Two boards dominate IGCSE in Dubai schools, and they examine the same subjects differently enough that past papers do not transfer. Cambridge Mathematics 0580 now sets a non-calculator paper worth half the grade; Pearson Mathematics Specification A, 4MA1, permits a calculator in both of its two-hour papers. Cambridge separate sciences run a dedicated multiple-choice paper and a practical component the school chooses between a laboratory test and an alternative-to-practical written paper; Pearson has no separate practical examination and assesses those skills inside the written papers. Cambridge International Mathematics 0607 is a different syllabus from 0580 rather than a variant of it, and assumes a graphics calculator throughout.

A tutor who does not establish the code will teach the subject well and prepare the wrong examination. That failure is quiet. The student understands the lessons, the parent hears competent teaching, the homework gets done, and in March the student meets a paper structured differently from every paper they have practised. Nobody involved did anything negligent, and a term is gone. This is the single most common form of wasted IGCSE tutoring money we see in this district, and it costs nothing to prevent.

The prevention is documentary rather than intuitive. There are five documents, all of them obtainable from your child's school or already somewhere in the house, that between them establish board, syllabus code, tier, series and - for Cambridge sciences - which practical route is entered. With those in hand, a conversation with any prospective tutor takes two minutes and the answer is checkable rather than reassuring. They are listed in a table below and we would rather hand them over than ask anybody to trust a claim, including ours.

On delivery, since the URL says home tutor and that is the phrase parents type: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. Home visits are a service we provide only in India. Every lesson for an Oud Metha family is one-to-one over live video in a Gulf Standard Time slot, and we hold no office, centre or branch anywhere in the UAE. The board-matching problem is actually the clearest argument for that model: a specialist in Pearson 4MB1 or Cambridge 0607 is defined by the examination, not by whether they can reach Oud Metha before five.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-oud-metha.programmesIntro: The four things to pin down before hiring anyone. Each is a fact, each is obtainable, and each changes what a tutor should be doing.

programmes.name: Cambridge International or Pearson Edexcel
programmes.description: The school chooses, sometimes differently by subject, so a single household can be dealing with both at once. Cambridge reports A* to G on some syllabuses and 9 to 1 on others depending on the school's choice; Pearson International GCSE reports 9 to 1. Grade scales, paper structures and practical arrangements all follow from this one fact, and it is the first question to ask.
programmes.countryNote: In Dubai both boards are well represented because UK curriculum accounts for 37 per cent of private school enrolment. That depth is good news for supply and bad news for assumption: never infer the board from the school's reputation or from a sibling's experience.

programmes.name: The syllabus code
programmes.description: The four-character identifier that defines the examination: 0580 or 0607 for Cambridge mathematics, 4MA1 or 4MB1 for Pearson, 0620 or 4CH1 for chemistry, 0654 or 4SD0 for a double science award. It is printed on the examination entry and the subject department knows it. Without it a tutor is choosing past papers by subject name, which is how the mismatch happens.
programmes.countryNote: This is the single most useful thing a Dubai parent can write down. Keep the codes for all nine or ten subjects in one note on a phone; every conversation with a tutor, a sixth form or a revision site gets shorter and more accurate.

programmes.name: The tier entered
programmes.description: Cambridge splits into Core and Extended; Pearson splits into Foundation, covering grades 5 to 1, and Higher, covering 9 to 4 with an allowed grade 3. The lower tier carries a hard ceiling that no amount of tutoring lifts, and families frequently do not know the decision has been made. Ask in writing which tier each tiered subject is entered for and what the ceiling is.
programmes.countryNote: Schools make this call for defensible reasons - a student on a tier beyond their reach risks coming away with nothing. The problem is communication, not judgement. Ask what evidence the decision rested on and whether it can be reviewed, and ask early.

programmes.name: The series and the zone
programmes.description: UAE candidates sit June and November. The February and March series that appears in searches is offered to India only. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for your zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong version.
programmes.countryNote: Take the timetable from the school's exams office rather than from a search result. Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series and revises them, so the live official timetable is the only one worth planning from.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-oud-metha.subjectsIntro: The main IGCSE subjects with both boards' codes alongside, because the code is what a tutor needs and the subject name is what families usually have.

subjects.name: Mathematics
subjects.description: Four distinct examinations. Cambridge 0580 sets a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper at 50 per cent each; 0607 International Mathematics assumes a graphics calculator and includes an investigation component; Pearson 4MA1 runs two two-hour calculator papers; 4MB1 is Specification B with papers of unequal length. Getting this code wrong is the costliest mismatch available.

subjects.name: Physics
subjects.description: Cambridge runs a multiple-choice paper, a theory paper and a practical component the school selects. Pearson sets a longer first paper and a shorter second, with practical skills assessed inside them and no separate practical examination. A Cambridge candidate needs timed multiple-choice practice as its own skill; a Pearson candidate needs stamina on the long paper.

subjects.name: Chemistry
subjects.description: Same structural difference as physics, plus different emphases in the quantitative content. Both reward the mole and reacting-mass chain heavily, so a tutor diagnosing a chemistry problem should check that chain first - but they must do it with questions from the right board, because the question style differs noticeably.

subjects.name: Biology
subjects.description: The largest content volume of the three sciences on either board, and marked on precision of terminology. The required wording differs in places between boards, which means mark-scheme wording drills are only useful if they come from the board the student is actually sitting.

subjects.name: Coordinated and combined science
subjects.description: Double and single award routes covering all three disciplines in fewer qualifications. These are the codes most often mistaken for separate sciences, and the mismatch is severe: a student on 0654 practising 0625 physics papers is working on content and depth that are not on their syllabus at all.

subjects.name: English Language
subjects.description: Directed writing, descriptive and narrative tasks and reading response work, with different task types and mark allocations by board. Cambridge also offers both a legacy-lettered and a 9 to 1 version, which is a further reason to confirm the code rather than the subject name.

subjects.name: English Literature
subjects.description: Both reward close analysis of a writer's choices with quotation embedded rather than appended, and both penalise plot retelling. The set texts differ by school and by board, so a tutor must be working on the actual texts rather than on a generic approach to literature.

subjects.name: Economics and Business
subjects.description: Diagram accuracy, precise technical vocabulary and application to the stimulus rather than recitation. Evaluation questions need a judgement rather than a balanced list. Mark allocations and question styles differ by board enough that practising the wrong one builds the wrong habits.

subjects.name: History and Geography
subjects.description: Both boards use source or data-based components alongside extended writing, with different source-question formats. History rewards evaluating sources for origin, purpose, value and limitation. Geography rewards case-study specificity - named places, named figures, named consequences - and the required case studies are school-specific.

subjects.name: Computer Science and ICT
subjects.description: Theory papers rewarding precise technical definition plus practical or pseudocode components. Pseudocode conventions differ by board, which is an unusually concrete example of why the code matters: a student writing one board's pseudocode style in the other board's paper loses marks for formatting.

subjects.name: Further and Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Taken alongside the main mathematics by students heading for A Level or Diploma Higher Level mathematics, introducing calculus. Also the subject most often quietly dropped when a Year 11 week overflows, which is a decision worth making deliberately in Year 10.

subjects.name: Arabic and additional languages
subjects.description: Separate from the mandatory Arabic provision a Dubai school runs, and examined across reading, writing, listening and speaking with board-specific formats. The speaking component is the one students prepare least and it responds to short frequent rehearsal rather than long sessions.

sections.heading: Five documents that prove what your child is actually sitting
paragraphs: Everything on this page depends on facts a web page cannot supply, so here is how to get them. Five documents, all obtainable, between them establish the board, the syllabus code, the tier, the series and the practical route for every subject. Collecting them takes one email and a search through a school bag, and it is the cheapest useful hour a Year 10 or Year 11 parent will spend.

The examination entry statement is the most authoritative of them. It lists what the school has entered your child for, by board and code, and it is the document a tutor should be shown rather than told about. Many Dubai schools issue a statement of entry for the candidate to check, which is itself an invitation to check it - and checking it is worth doing carefully, because an entry error caught early is fixable and one caught in June is not.

After that, the subject booklet or course outline each department issues at the start of the course usually names the syllabus and sometimes the code. The marked mock script carries the paper reference at the top, which identifies the code even where nothing else does. The school's reporting documentation often states the qualification being worked towards. And a direct email to the head of department settles anything the paperwork leaves ambiguous, including which Cambridge practical route is entered and which tier applies.

One practical suggestion. Put the results in a single note on a phone: subject, board, code, tier, series. Nine or ten lines. Every subsequent conversation - with a tutor, with a sixth form, with a revision website, with a relative offering advice - becomes faster and more accurate, and the mismatch risk disappears. Families in Oud Metha who do this tend to be the ones who do not waste a term, and it is not because they know more about the subjects.

sections.heading: Cambridge against Pearson Edexcel, subject by subject
paragraphs: Families generally know that two boards exist and assume the difference is cosmetic. It is not, and the differences are concrete enough to list. The point of the table below is not that one board is harder - it is that a tutor working from the wrong one prepares the wrong thing while appearing to do the right thing.

Mathematics is the sharpest case. Cambridge 0580 now sets one non-calculator paper and one calculator paper, each worth 50 per cent, which means a Cambridge candidate must handle fractions, surds, indices and long arithmetic cleanly by hand under time pressure. Pearson 4MA1 permits a calculator in both of its two-hour, 100-mark papers, so marks tend to go on method, question-reading and stamina instead. A student drilled on one profile and sitting the other is underprepared in a specific, predictable way.

The sciences differ on the practical component and on multiple choice. Cambridge separate sciences run a dedicated multiple-choice paper - a distinct timed skill that needs its own practice - and a practical component the school chooses between a laboratory test and an alternative-to-practical written paper. Pearson sets no separate multiple-choice paper and no separate practical examination, assessing practical and investigative skills inside the written papers. So a Pearson candidate meets experimental questions mixed into theory and should treat them as ordinary revision rather than a separate block.

Elsewhere the differences are smaller individually and still real: pseudocode conventions differ in computer science, so formatting marks are at stake; mark allocations and question styles differ in economics and business; required mark-scheme wording differs in places in biology; source-question formats differ in history. And the grade scales differ, with Pearson International GCSE on 9 to 1 and Cambridge on either A* to G or 9 to 1 depending on the syllabus - which is why two children in one Oud Metha household can bring home reports that are not comparable.

sections.heading: What a board mismatch actually looks like from the next room
paragraphs: The reason this failure persists is that it is invisible while it is happening. It is worth describing precisely, because recognising the pattern is what lets a parent stop it in week two rather than in March.

A tutor is hired for physics. They are a good physics teacher. They explain circuits clearly, the student follows, homework improves, and the parent hearing the session from the next room has every reason to be satisfied. The tutor is working from Cambridge 0625 past papers because that is what they have taught most and because nobody told them otherwise. The student is on Pearson 4PH1. Nothing in the weekly experience reveals the problem: the physics is the same physics, the explanations are right, and the student's understanding genuinely improves.

What goes wrong appears at the assessment. The student has had no timed multiple-choice practice because Pearson sets no multiple-choice paper, so that was never relevant - but equally they have had no practice on Pearson's long first paper, with its particular distribution of marks and its practical questions mixed into theory. The question styles are unfamiliar, the stamina demand is different, and the marks do not reflect the understanding. Everybody then concludes the student does not cope under pressure, which is the wrong diagnosis, and the following term is spent on exam nerves rather than on the actual problem.

There are two tells a parent can watch for without subject knowledge. First, ask to see what past-paper material is being used and look at the paper reference printed at the top - it will name a code, and it should be your child's code. Second, listen for the tutor asking the student about the structure of their own paper. A tutor who is working from the right code refers to the specific papers your child will sit, by number and content. A tutor who never mentions them is teaching the subject rather than the examination.
bullets: The weekly experience looks fine, because the subject teaching genuinely is fine
The failure only appears at the assessment, and gets misdiagnosed as exam nerves

sections.heading: Two boards in one Oud Metha household
paragraphs: This district has several large schools within a short radius, which means something slightly unusual: households here frequently have children at different schools, and therefore on different boards, sometimes with different grade scales. That creates a specific set of confusions worth untangling.

The first is report comparison. Pearson International GCSE reports on the 9 to 1 scale. Cambridge reports A* to G on some syllabuses and 9 to 1 on others depending on the school's choice. A parent looking at one child's 7 and another's B is not comparing like with like, and well-meaning comparisons between siblings on that basis are both unfair and uninformative. Ask each school which scale applies, and ask for the tier alongside it, because a 6 on a higher tier and a 6 on a lower tier do not mean the same thing either.

The second is shared revision material. Siblings naturally share books, notes and websites, and in this case sharing can actively harm. A past paper that is right for one child is wrong for the other. A revision guide written for one board teaches the wrong practical arrangement to the other. The simplest fix is labelling: keep each child's material physically separate and write the board and code on the front of everything.

The third is the assumption that one tutor can serve both. Occasionally the content overlap makes that workable for a subject where the examination differences are small. More often it produces a tutor who does the familiar board properly and the other board approximately, and the second child quietly gets the worse service. Two specialists scheduled across the week is more work to arrange and it is what we recommend, which is also why we schedule households rather than individuals when a family tells us there is more than one child involved.

sections.heading: What a tutor should ask you in the first five minutes
paragraphs: The verification runs both ways. A tutor who is doing this properly will interrogate you before teaching anything, and the absence of those questions is itself diagnostic. Here is what a competent first contact sounds like from the parent's side.

They should ask for the board and syllabus code, by subject, and not accept the subject name as sufficient. They should ask which tier is entered for each tiered subject, and what the ceiling is, because that determines whether a target grade is even available. They should ask which series the student is entered for. For Cambridge sciences they should ask whether the practical test or the alternative-to-practical written paper is entered, because those are prepared for differently. And they should ask for a marked script rather than a list of topics the student finds difficult.

They should also ask something about the calendar: when the next school assessment falls, when the reports are issued, and whether mocks have happened. Those dates are what a plan is aimed at, and a tutor who starts teaching without knowing them is producing a generic sequence rather than a plan. In our first contact we ask for all of it, and if a family does not have the answers we ask them to get them before the trial rather than guessing in the trial.

What a tutor should not do is claim certainty they cannot have. Nobody can tell you from outside the school which code your child is on, which tier they are entered for, or which practical route applies. A tutor who states those things confidently without having been told has guessed, and a guess that happens to be right is still a process that will eventually be wrong. We would rather ask five questions and look less impressive than assert something and be wrong about a term of a child's work.
bullets: Board and code by subject, never the subject name alone
Tier and ceiling for each tiered subject

sections.heading: When the tutor is right and the problem is somewhere else
paragraphs: Having argued for nine sections that matching matters, honesty requires the other half: sometimes the board is right, the tutor is right, and the problem is elsewhere entirely. A family that spends money on tutoring when the issue is load, sleep or availability of free support has solved nothing and feels worse about it.

Load first. A Dubai IGCSE week carries nine or ten subjects plus mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral studies, which are required in all Dubai private schools whatever international curriculum the school is licensed for, with instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit and KHDA advising a minimum of 25 minutes per mandatory subject lesson. Those are real hours in an already full week. A student failing to complete work across several subjects may be describing arithmetic rather than ability, and adding a tutoring hour subtracts from the same finite week.

Free support second, and this matters particularly in Oud Metha. Sitting inside the school belt means departmental revision sessions, after-school clinics and teacher availability are physically easy to reach, and they are free. Before paying anybody it is worth establishing exactly what the school runs and when. We would rather a family used a free departmental session than bought an hour from us covering the same ground, and we will say so when the free option looks adequate for what is actually wrong.

Third, the problem is sometimes simply that work does not get done, in which case supervision is the honest purchase rather than subject teaching - and supervision is what the budget end of this market actually sells, at AED 33 to 52 an hour from Tutopiya and AED 45 to 65 from EdFlik as read in October 2026. Paying a specialist rate for somebody to sit with a student while they do homework they could do unaided is the most expensive way to solve a behavioural problem. A two or three session diagnosis will tell you which of these three you have, and occasionally the answer is that no tutoring is required.

sections.heading: What code-matched IGCSE tutoring costs in this market
paragraphs: A fair question at this point is whether matching the exact code costs more, and the answer is that it narrows who you can hire without changing the band you should be paying in. The market figures below are each attributed and were read in October 2026 from the provider's own pages.

At the budget end, Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65. That band buys homework supervision, which as noted above is sometimes exactly the right purchase. Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 an hour. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table places IGCSE, IB and A-Level specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above; TutorChase publishes AED 270; BartyED sits at AED 650 for premium named tutors. In-home one-to-one visits including travel are quoted at AED 180 to 350 by Bestimate and up to AED 500 by independent home tutors. Monthly, Bestimate estimates a weekly one-hour session at AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year work, with packages advertised around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour in-home sessions.

Where the code genuinely justifies the specialist band is anything structural: paper technique for a specific paper, mock-script diagnosis, and the less common codes such as Cambridge 0607 or Pearson 4MB1 where the examination differs substantially from the mainstream version. Where it does not is content explanation of material that is the same on both boards - quadratic equations are quadratic equations, and a competent mid-band tutor teaching them is giving you the same thing as a specialist at twice the price, provided the practice questions come from the right code.

None of these are IB Gram prices; we publish no rate card on a landing page and would rather quote against an actual requirement. We hold no office, centre or branch in the UAE, and we are not approved, accredited, licensed or partnered by KHDA, Cambridge International, Pearson or anyone else. We publish no satisfaction percentage, star rating or tutor headcount either, because none of those could carry a sample size, a date and a method. Two questions for any provider including us: is the rate per hour or per lesson, and what happens if you stop after one session.

sections.heading: What you can see, and what you can keep
paragraphs: The in-home instinct is partly about oversight, and that is worth addressing on its own terms rather than through a cost comparison. A parent wants to know what happened in the hour. In a flat or a villa, the way you know is by being nearby and listening. It works, up to a point, and the point is that listening tells you the tone of a session rather than its content.

Our position, stated before anyone pays: IB Gram does not send tutors to homes anywhere in the UAE. Home visits are a service we provide only in India. Every lesson for an Oud Metha family is one-to-one over live video in a Gulf Standard Time slot, and we hold no office or premises in the UAE. We put that on the page because two providers ranking for these searches route UAE parents to overseas phone numbers without disclosing where the tutor actually sits, and a family should know before paying rather than after.

What the online format substitutes for listening is a record. Session notes after each lesson, saying which paper and which topic were worked on. Shared annotated material that persists - a marked past-paper question with the tutor's own working on it, which the student can look at again before the next assessment and which a parent can read. For a board-matching worry specifically, that record is the strongest form of oversight available, because the code is printed on the material and you can see it. Listening from the next room cannot tell you which board's paper is on the table.

The practical gains are the ordinary ones and they apply with particular force here. The hour holds, because nobody travels. A different specialist can serve each board in a two-board household within the same week. If a tutor's availability changes mid-term, the slot can be rematched within days rather than ending the arrangement. And Oud Metha's genuinely short commute - the best in Old Dubai - makes an early 4pm or 4.30pm slot realistic, which is an advantage of the district that applies equally to a session on a screen.

sections.heading: The regulator, equivalency and the permit you can check
paragraphs: Dubai's private schools are overseen by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which is responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate and inspects on a six-band scale from Outstanding down to Very Weak. In 2024-25 the sector was 387,441 students across 227 private schools offering seventeen different curricula, with UK curriculum at 37 per cent of students and Indian at 26 per cent - which is why both IGCSE boards are deeply represented here. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees in Dubai for the 2026-27 academic year, under the emirate's second economic incentives package valued at AED 1.5 billion within a AED 2.5 billion total.

Across the other emirates the regulator differs, which matters for a family that may move. Abu Dhabi and Al Ain fall under the Department of Education and Knowledge, which supervises the licensing and accreditation of private schools there. Sharjah has the Sharjah Private Education Authority and Ras Al Khaimah its own Department of Knowledge, and in both emirates the authority approves tuition fees, curricula, programmes, courses, activities and assessment methods rather than only inspecting. The Ministry of Education supervises private schools in Ajman, Umm Al Quwain and Fujairah.

On equivalency, which bears directly on how many subjects are entered: the Ministry of Education's British track requires a student to pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3, and to show one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than grade E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects. One ranking competitor publishes a six-subject requirement; the sourced figure is five. Verify your own case through the Ministry's own channel - we describe the process, do not perform or guarantee it, and tutoring is not a requirement of it.

On permits, the position is checkable and worth adding to your document collection. The MoHRE private tuition work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 and is granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's own service page is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fees and states a two-working-day completion time, applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system. Tutoring without a permit attracts fines and penalties under the applicable laws, and because no fine schedule is published officially, nobody should quote you an amount. We also do not host or redistribute Cambridge or Pearson past papers, mark schemes, grade-boundary tables or syllabus documents - we cite them and link out, because they are the boards' copyright.

faqs.question: How do I find out which exam board my child's IGCSEs are with?
faqs.answer: Five documents settle it. The statement of entry from the exams office is authoritative and lists board, syllabus code, tier and series per subject. Each department's course outline usually names the syllabus. A marked mock script carries the paper reference printed at the top. The report documentation often states the qualification. And one email to each head of department resolves anything ambiguous, including which Cambridge practical route is entered. Write the results in a single note: subject, board, code, tier, series.

faqs.question: Is a four-character code really more important than the subject title?
faqs.answer: Because the code defines the examination and the subject name does not. Cambridge Mathematics 0580 sets a non-calculator paper worth half the grade; Cambridge International Mathematics 0607 assumes a graphics calculator and includes an investigation; Pearson 4MA1 runs two two-hour calculator papers; Pearson 4MB1 is a different specification again. All four are called IGCSE Mathematics. A tutor choosing past papers by subject name has a one-in-four chance of using the right ones, and the mistake is quiet.

faqs.question: What actually goes wrong if a tutor uses the wrong board's papers?
faqs.answer: The teaching is fine and the preparation is wrong, which is why it goes unnoticed. The physics is the same physics and the explanations are right, so the weekly experience looks good. What the student never gets is practice on the paper they will actually sit - its question styles, its mark distribution, its stamina demand, whether it contains a multiple-choice section, whether practical questions are mixed into theory. The marks then fail to reflect the understanding, and everyone misdiagnoses it as exam nerves.

faqs.question: What are the two things I can check without knowing the subject?
faqs.answer: First, look at the past-paper material being used: the code is printed at the top of the paper, and it should match your child's code. That is a direct, decisive check requiring no subject knowledge at all. Second, listen for whether the tutor refers to your child's actual papers by number and content - a tutor working from the right code talks about Paper 1 and Paper 2 specifically, because the structure determines the teaching. A tutor who never mentions them is teaching a subject rather than an examination.

faqs.question: Is Cambridge or Pearson Edexcel IGCSE harder?
faqs.answer: Neither, and the question is less useful than it seems because the school has already chosen. What matters is that they differ structurally. Cambridge separate sciences include a dedicated multiple-choice paper and a practical component the school selects between a laboratory test and an alternative-to-practical written paper. Pearson sets no separate practical examination and assesses those skills inside the written papers. Cambridge Mathematics now sets a non-calculator paper; Pearson permits calculators throughout. Those differences change revision, not difficulty.

faqs.question: My two children are on different boards. Can one tutor cover both?
faqs.answer: Sometimes for a subject where the examination differences are small, but it usually produces one board served properly and the other approximately, with the second child quietly getting the worse service. Two specialists across the week is more work to arrange and is what we recommend. There are two other things to fix in a two-board household: do not share past papers or revision guides between the children, and label every book and note with its board and code.

faqs.question: Why can't I compare my children's IGCSE grades directly?
faqs.answer: Because the scales may differ. Pearson International GCSE reports on 9 to 1. Cambridge reports A* to G on some syllabuses and 9 to 1 on others, depending on the school's choice. So one child's 7 and another's B are not comparable. The tier compounds it: a 6 on a higher tier and a 6 on a lower tier are different achievements, because the lower tier carries a grade ceiling. Ask each school which scale applies and which tier is entered, and compare nothing until you have both.

faqs.question: What should a tutor ask me in the first five minutes?
faqs.answer: Board and syllabus code by subject, never the subject name alone. Which tier is entered for each tiered subject and what the ceiling is. Which series the student sits. For Cambridge sciences, whether the practical test or the alternative-to-practical paper is entered. And for a marked script rather than a list of difficult topics. They should also ask when the next school assessment and report fall, because that is what a plan is aimed at. The absence of those questions is itself diagnostic.

faqs.question: Can a tutor tell me which code my child is on?
faqs.answer: No, and one who states it confidently has guessed. Nobody outside the school can know which syllabus code your child is entered for, which tier applies, or which Cambridge practical route the school chose. Those facts live in the entry and in the department. A tutor who asserts them without being told has used a process that will eventually be wrong about somebody's term of work. We would rather ask five questions and look less impressive than assert something and be wrong.

faqs.question: Do you send an IGCSE tutor to a home in Oud Metha?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not provide home visits anywhere in the UAE; home visits are a service we run only in India. Every lesson for an Oud Metha family is one-to-one over live video in a Gulf Standard Time slot, and we hold no office, centre or branch in the UAE either. For a board-matching worry the online format actually gives stronger oversight, because the code is printed on shared material you can read - listening from the next room cannot tell you which board's paper is on the table.

faqs.question: Does matching the exact syllabus code cost more?
faqs.answer: It narrows who you can hire rather than changing the band you should pay in. Market rates read in October 2026: Unitors publishes IGCSE from AED 150 an hour, Bestimate's Dubai table places specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, TutorChase publishes AED 270, and the budget end runs AED 33 to 65. The specialist band is justified for paper technique, mock-script diagnosis and the less common codes such as 0607 or 4MB1. For content that is the same on both boards, a competent mid-band tutor suffices - with the right practice questions.

faqs.question: What if the week is simply too full for another hour?
faqs.answer: Then another hour subtracts from the same finite week, and we would rather tell you. A Dubai IGCSE week carries nine or ten subjects plus mandatory Arabic, Islamic Education and Social or Moral studies, required in all Dubai private schools whatever the licensed curriculum, with instructional time calculated on a 40-minute lesson unit and a minimum advised 25 minutes per lesson. A student failing to complete work across several subjects may be describing arithmetic. A two or three session diagnosis establishes which it is cheaply.

faqs.question: Could the school's own support be enough instead of paying a tutor?
faqs.answer: Often, and it is worth checking first in a district like this one. Oud Metha sits inside the school belt, so departmental revision sessions, after-school clinics and teacher availability are physically easy to reach and cost nothing. Establish exactly what the school runs and when before paying anybody. Where the free option looks adequate for what is actually wrong, we will say so rather than take the booking - a family that trusts the first recommendation is there for the second.

faqs.question: My child had a tutor before and it did not work. What should I look at?
faqs.answer: Check the board first, because a mismatch in a previous arrangement is one of the commonest explanations and it is quick to confirm. If you still have any past-paper material from those sessions, look at the code printed on it. The second thing to check is whether the help went to a subject where the problem was content, when the actual losses were technique - wrong command word, too few creditable points, no working shown. A short diagnostic engagement against the correct mark scheme usually identifies which.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE series do Oud Metha students sit?
faqs.answer: June and November. Cambridge runs June as the main series with November as the resit route for UAE centres, and Pearson International GCSE is available in May/June and November. The February and March series that appears in searches is offered to India only and does not apply here. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states it is essential to use the correct timetable version for that zone, so take the timetable from the exams office rather than from a search result.

faqs.question: Does a tutor working with an Oud Metha family need a UAE permit?
faqs.answer: Yes, and it belongs in your document collection alongside the syllabus codes. Private tutoring in the UAE requires the MoHRE private tuition work permit introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, granted free of charge for two years. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students and school students aged 15 to 18. MoHRE's service page lists no fee and a two-working-day completion time. Since the permit costs nothing, there is no reason not to hold one.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-oud-metha.closingHeading: Collect five documents, then hire with confidence
dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-oud-metha.closingBody: The worry behind this search is the right one, and it has a documentary answer rather than a reassuring one. Get the statement of entry, the course outlines, a marked mock script and one email per head of department, and write the result in a single note: subject, board, code, tier, series. With that note in hand, any tutor conversation takes two minutes and you can verify the answer rather than trust it - including ours, by looking at the code printed on the shared material. Then take the free trial on the correct paper. All lessons for Oud Metha families are one-to-one over live video, and we do not send tutors to UAE addresses.

intro.heading: The money question, answered before the sales pitch
paragraphs: A family on Palm Jumeirah deciding to hire an IGCSE home tutor is weighing a recurring cost against an uncertain benefit, usually in a hurry, usually with incomplete information. The incomplete information is not an accident. Of the best-ranking pages researched for this project, three publish no price at all, and two of the three that do quote in US dollars, which is not the currency a Dubai family transacts in. One agency's own frequently asked questions ask what tutoring costs and then decline to answer.

So here are the dirham figures, taken from providers' own public pages in October 2026 and attributed to each. Budget online platforms advertise from AED 33 to 52 at Tutopiya and AED 45 to 65 at EdFlik. Unitors publishes from AED 150 an hour for IGCSE and AED 200 for IB. TutorChase lists AED 270. The Bestimate Dubai rate guide puts specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, and in-home visits at AED 180 to 350, with individual home tutors advertising up to AED 500. BartyED sits at AED 650 at the premium end. Monthly packages in the market include around AED 799 for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 for four two-hour home visits.

Those numbers describe the market, not an IB Gram price list. We quote per student after a free trial lesson and a short diagnostic, because an hourly rate quoted before anybody has seen the child's marked work is a guess dressed up as a price. What this page can do is make the spread legible: why one hour costs five times another, which part of the higher number is teaching and which part is a car on the Palm trunk at 6pm, and where families routinely pay for something that was never going to move a grade.

The waste patterns are consistent and expensive. A group class bought for a diagnosed individual gap. Two hours booked because a travelling tutor has a two-hour minimum, when the child's concentration runs out at sixty-five minutes. A term of weekly sessions started without anybody establishing what was wrong, so the first six hours go on revisiting topics the student already had. Past-paper drilling with no marking against the published mark scheme, which teaches a student to be faster at the same mistakes. And the one nobody expects: paying for a tutor who does not know which board the school entered the child for.

The rest of the page works through all of it. There is a rate table by level and format, a breakdown of where the money inside a single hour actually goes, a Cambridge against Pearson Edexcel comparison with syllabus codes because the board changes the work, the cost of tuition set beside Dubai school fees and the KHDA fee freeze, a list of questions to ask before any money moves, and an honest account of how to buy fewer hours rather than more. IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE; Palm Jumeirah families are taught one-to-one over live video, which is also why no part of the hour you pay for is spent driving.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-palm-jumeirah.programmesIntro: Palm Jumeirah families sit their children in schools that pick their own qualification routes, and the route decides both the work and the cost. These are the three stages where island parents most often start paying for support, with what each one demands.

programmes.name: Cambridge IGCSE
programmes.description: A two-year course examined by Cambridge International in a June series and a November series, with syllabus codes that identify the exact course: 0580 for Mathematics, 0620 Chemistry, 0625 Physics, 0610 Biology, 0500 English as a First Language. Many subjects are tiered, so the school's decision between Core and Extended entry sets the grade ceiling. Every exam centre is allocated to one of six administrative zones, and the zone determines which version of the timetable applies.
programmes.countryNote: For a Palm Jumeirah family the cost consequence of tiering is the one worth understanding. A student entered for Core cannot reach the top grades whatever the tutoring spend, so money spent on a Core candidate buys security rather than a higher ceiling. The conversation with the school about tier, usually in Year 10, is worth more than a term of sessions and costs nothing.

programmes.name: Pearson Edexcel International GCSE
programmes.description: Pearson's international qualification, examined in May/June and November each year, with its own codes: 4MA1 Mathematics A, 4CH1 Chemistry, 4PH1 Physics, 4BI1 Biology, 4EA1 English Language A. Papers, tiering and content differ from the Cambridge equivalent even where the subject name matches, and Pearson publishes provisional timetables ahead of each series, so dates can be revised before they are final.
programmes.countryNote: Island families with children in two different schools frequently have two different boards in the same house. That is a real budgeting issue: the same subject at the same level needs a tutor who knows the specific board's papers, and buying one tutor for both children only works if that tutor genuinely covers both. Ask for the code, not the subject name.

programmes.name: The post-16 decision and the year before it
programmes.description: The IGCSE year ends in a choice between A Levels and the IB Diploma, and the grades obtained decide which doors stay open. Several Dubai schools set subject-specific entry requirements for their own sixth form. For Ministry of Education equivalency on the British track, students must show five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade no lower than E or grade 3, with Arabic and Islamic education not counted among the five.
programmes.countryNote: The cost argument for support in Year 11 rather than Year 12 is simple: a grade recovered at IGCSE is cheaper than a subject repeated or a sixth-form place lost. Families who spend in Year 11 tend to spend less in total. Equivalency rules should always be checked on the Ministry's own channels, and no IB points threshold should be relied upon from a secondary source.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-palm-jumeirah.subjectsIntro: These are the IGCSE subjects Palm Jumeirah families most often pay for, with the syllabus code where it identifies the course and the specific thing that usually needs fixing. The code matters because it tells a tutor which papers your child will actually sit.

subjects.name: Mathematics (Cambridge 0580, Edexcel 4MA1)
subjects.levels: Core and Extended, or Foundation and Higher
subjects.description: The highest-volume request in Dubai and the one where tier choice decides the ceiling. Extended papers reward algebraic fluency and multi-step problems; marks go missing on method not shown and on questions that need a worded conclusion. A diagnostic on one past paper tells you more than three weeks of general revision.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics (Cambridge 0606) and International Mathematics (0607)
subjects.description: Taken by students heading for a demanding post-16 maths route, often as a bridge to Higher Level. The content is substantially harder than 0580 and the tutoring market for it is thinner, so expect a smaller pool and plan earlier. Confusing 0580, 0606 and 0607 when booking is a common and expensive mistake.

subjects.name: Physics (Cambridge 0625, Edexcel 4PH1)
subjects.description: Electricity and circuits are where most Dubai students lose marks, followed by anything requiring a rearranged equation under time pressure. Practical skills are assessed on a written paper rather than in a laboratory, which means they can be taught online with paper questions and graph work.

subjects.name: Chemistry (Cambridge 0620, Edexcel 4CH1)
subjects.description: Moles, ionic equations and organic nomenclature account for a large share of dropped marks. Students who have learned definitions without practising calculation score inconsistently. Marking one paper against the published mark scheme usually reveals whether the problem is content or precision.

subjects.name: Biology (Cambridge 0610, Edexcel 4BI1)
subjects.description: High content volume tempts families into buying more hours than the subject needs. The marks are usually lost to command-word errors and to answers that describe when they should explain. Structured recall practice between sessions is what makes the paid hour worth paying for.

subjects.name: Combined and Coordinated Sciences (Cambridge 0653, 0654)
subjects.description: Three sciences compressed into fewer papers, often taken by students who will not continue sciences post-16. The budget question here is whether to hire one tutor across all three, which works only if the tutor genuinely teaches all three at this level rather than one well and two approximately.

subjects.name: English as a First Language (Cambridge 0500, Edexcel 4EA1)
subjects.description: Reading comprehension and directed writing carry the marks, and both are technique-led rather than knowledge-led. This is the subject where a small number of well-marked practice pieces outperforms a long weekly commitment, which makes it one of the cheapest grades to move.

subjects.name: English as a Second Language (Cambridge 0510)
subjects.description: A different qualification from first-language English with different papers and a speaking component. Island households with more than one home language sometimes discover mid-year that the child has been entered for the wrong one of the two, which is worth confirming with the school before spending anything.

subjects.name: Economics (0455) and Business Studies (0450)
subjects.description: Definitions and diagrams earn the early marks; the longer responses need application to the case material and a judgement at the end. Most tutoring time is spent on content when it should be spent on structuring eight and twelve-mark answers against the mark scheme.

subjects.name: Computer Science (0478) and ICT (0417)
subjects.description: Two very different subjects routinely confused when booking. Computer Science rewards algorithmic thinking and pseudocode discipline; ICT is practical and application-based. Paying for a tutor in the wrong one of the two is a mistake families usually notice at the second session.

dubai/igcse-home-tutor-in-palm-jumeirah.regionsTitle: Palm Jumeirah by address, and what each part does to a tutoring budget

regions.name: The fronds
regions.note: Sixteen residential spurs reached one at a time from the trunk, with no through route between them. A tutor driving to a villa here adds the frond itself to the journey each way, which is exactly the time an in-home rate is built to recover.
