intro.heading: What an IGCSE maths problem actually looks like at Year 10 and 11
paragraphs: A parent in Al Barsha South rarely arrives with a vague worry. The trigger is specific: a mock paper came back at a grade 5 when the school had predicted a 7, or the calculator paper went fine and the non-calculator paper collapsed, or the student can factorise anything you put in front of them and still cannot read a worded question about a cumulative frequency curve. Those three complaints have three different causes, and they need three different terms of work. Treating them all as "needs more maths" is how a family spends eight months paying for revision that never touches the thing that is actually losing marks.

Start from the paper structure, because the structure is what decides where marks go missing. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 splits into a Core tier, graded C to G, and an Extended tier, graded A* to E. Extended candidates sit Paper 2, a non-calculator paper, and Paper 4, where a calculator is allowed. Core candidates sit Paper 1 and Paper 3 on the same split. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A, syllabus 4MA1, works differently again: two papers of equal weight, a calculator permitted throughout, Foundation tier capped at grade 5 and Higher tier running 9 to 4. A student who has spent a year on a graphics-display calculator and is then put into a non-calculator paper has a mechanical problem, not a conceptual one, and the fix is drill, not re-teaching.

The second structural fact is the command term. IGCSE mathematics mark schemes do not award marks for an answer that happens to be right. They award method marks, accuracy marks and, in the longer parts, marks for a correct statement that leads nowhere. A student who writes down the final number with no working is throwing away between one and four marks on almost every multi-step question in Paper 4. This is the single most common diagnosable problem in the Al Barsha South students we see, and it is the fastest to fix, because it is a habit rather than a gap.

The third is topic sequencing. The 0580 Extended syllabus is wide: number, algebra and graphs, co-ordinate geometry, geometry, mensuration, trigonometry, transformations and vectors, probability and statistics. Schools in this part of Dubai typically finish the content by February of Year 11 and then revise. That means a student who is behind in November is behind on content that will not be retaught, and the tutoring has to run two tracks at once: catch up the gap while keeping pace with class. Running one track and hoping is how a student arrives at the final term with both problems instead of one.

What a tutoring plan should produce, by the end of the first month, is a written list: the topics where accuracy is above 80%, the topics where method is sound but arithmetic fails, and the topics where the student cannot start. That list is what a past paper gives you and a conversation does not. It is also the only honest basis for deciding whether a family needs one session a week or two, and for how long. No tutor can promise a grade. A tutor can tell you, from a marked paper, exactly which marks are currently unreachable and what sequence of work would reach them.

programmes.countryNote: International Baccalaureate students make up 7% of Dubai private-school enrolment, and Dubai's 2026-27 intake adds three new IB schools. For an Al Barsha South family weighing A Level against IB Diploma after IGCSE, the mathematics route is usually the deciding factor, because AA HL is the most demanding of the four options and the hardest to recover from if the IGCSE foundation is thin.

programmes.description: The other post-16 route out of IGCSE in this cluster. Pure mathematics at AS assumes the whole of 0580 Extended algebra as automatic, and students who scraped an A on the calculator paper often find the first term of AS brutal. The gap is almost always algebraic manipulation speed rather than new content.
programmes.countryNote: Most British-curriculum schools near Al Barsha South offer A Level alongside or instead of the IB Diploma, and a few run both. dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-barsha-sou.subjectsIntro: Mathematics is the page, but the mark-scheme problems cluster by topic rather than by subject. These are the areas of the Extended and Higher syllabuses where Al Barsha South students most often lose marks they could reach, with what the examiner is actually testing in each.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation and rearrangement
subjects.description: Changing the subject of a formula, simplifying algebraic fractions, expanding triple brackets. Tested heavily on the non-calculator Paper 2 and used as a step inside almost every longer Paper 4 question, so a weakness here is invisible in a topic test and expensive in a full paper.

subjects.name: Quadratics: factorising, formula and completing the square
subjects.description: Three methods, each worth knowing because the paper sometimes dictates which one. Completing the square is the one most students skip and the one that carries turning-point and minimum-value questions. Marks go on the sign errors, not the concept.

subjects.name: Functions, graphs and transformations
subjects.description: Sketching, reading intersections, composite and inverse functions, and the four transformations applied to a named curve. Students who learned graphs on a calculator cannot sketch them by hand, which is precisely what the non-calculator paper asks.

subjects.name: Trigonometry beyond right angles
subjects.description: Sine rule, cosine rule, area of a triangle, bearings, and three-dimensional trigonometry. The ambiguous case of the sine rule is a reliable marks sink, as is forgetting that a bearing is measured clockwise from north as a three-figure number.

subjects.name: Mensuration and compound solids
subjects.description: Surface area and volume of cylinders, cones, spheres and the composite shapes made from them, plus similar-solid scale factors. The scale-factor relationship between length, area and volume is tested almost every series and answered wrongly almost as often.

subjects.name: Vectors and column notation
subjects.description: Vector arithmetic, magnitude, and the geometric proofs that ask a student to express one displacement in terms of two others. This topic appears late in most schemes of work, so a student who is behind in February often meets it for the first time in revision.

subjects.name: Probability: trees, Venn diagrams and conditionals
subjects.description: Without-replacement tree diagrams and conditional probability from a two-way table. The error is usually structural rather than arithmetic: the second branch probabilities are not adjusted, and every subsequent mark falls with it.

subjects.name: Statistics: cumulative frequency and histograms
subjects.description: Median and quartiles read from a cumulative frequency curve, interquartile range, and frequency density for unequal class widths. Frequency density is the single most reliably mishandled calculation in the statistics section of either board's Higher paper.

subjects.name: Indices, standard form and surds
subjects.description: Negative and fractional indices, manipulating standard form without a calculator, and rationalising a denominator. All three appear as single-mark opening parts, which makes them cheap marks to bank and cheap marks to lose.

subjects.name: Number: ratio, percentage change and reverse percentages
subjects.description: Compound interest, depreciation, and the reverse percentage question that gives the post-increase figure and asks for the original. Students divide when they should multiply, and the mark scheme gives no method mark for a reasonable-looking wrong route.

subjects.name: Sequences and nth-term rules
subjects.description: Linear, quadratic and geometric sequences, plus the generalisation questions that want an algebraic rule rather than the next three terms. Quadratic nth-term is examinable on Extended and is often skipped in school revision for time.

subjects.name: Worded multi-step problems
subjects.description: Not a topic but a format: six to eight marks, several stages, with the mathematics hidden behind a context about a water tank or a currency conversion. Practice here is about extracting the equation, which is a separate trainable skill from solving it.

sections.heading: Which syllabus your child is actually sitting, and why it changes the plan
paragraphs: An IGCSE maths tutor in Al Barsha South who does not ask for the syllabus code in the first five minutes is guessing. Three codes dominate this cluster and they examine different things. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580 is the most common: a non-calculator paper and a calculator paper, tiered into Core and Extended. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A, 4MA1, permits a calculator on both papers and tiers into Foundation and Higher on the 9 to 1 scale. Cambridge International Mathematics 0607 is the outlier, built around a graphics display calculator with an investigation-style paper, and it is the one most often mistaken for 0580 by families and by tutors.

The practical consequence is revision material. A student on 4MA1 working through 0580 Paper 2 non-calculator questions is practising a skill their paper will not test in that form, and a 0580 Extended student practising 4MA1 papers is working with a calculator on questions they will have to answer without one. Both arrangements feel productive and neither targets the actual assessment. The fix costs nothing: the exam board and tier are printed on the school's exam entry confirmation, and a parent can read it in thirty seconds.

Tier matters as much as board. A 0580 Core entry is capped at grade C, and a 4MA1 Foundation entry is capped at grade 5. If a student is aiming for A Level Mathematics or IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches, a capped entry closes that door before the exam is sat. The reverse mistake is also real: an Extended entry for a student consistently scoring below 40% on past papers can produce a lower grade than a Core entry would have, because the Extended paper offers fewer accessible marks. That decision deserves a marked paper behind it, which is exactly what a four-session diagnostic block produces.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go: a working diagnosis of a lost paper
paragraphs: Take a 0580 Extended Paper 4 marked at 54 out of 100. The grade that produces is not the useful number. The useful number is the split. In the students we diagnose from this part of Dubai, a 54 typically breaks down as roughly twelve marks lost to topics never properly learned, fourteen lost to arithmetic slips on method the student knew, eight lost to questions started and abandoned on time, and twelve lost to answers that were right with no working shown. Four causes, four different remedies, and only one of them is more teaching.

The working-not-shown category is the cheapest to recover and the one schools have least time to chase. An IGCSE mathematics mark scheme allocates M marks for a correct method and A marks for accuracy. A student who computes three steps mentally and writes one number gets the A mark if the number is right and nothing at all if it is wrong. Over a full paper that is a swing of ten to fifteen marks, which on most series is a grade. Training it takes about three weeks of consistent correction and no new mathematics whatsoever.

The abandoned-questions category is a timing problem and is diagnosable only under timed conditions. A student who practises untimed will never discover that they spend eleven minutes on a six-mark trigonometry question and then have nine minutes for the last three pages. Timed section practice, marked immediately, surfaces this in the first week. The arithmetic-slip category splits again: slips on the calculator paper are usually input errors worth drilling, and slips on the non-calculator paper are usually fluency gaps in fractions, negatives and indices that need targeted drill rather than topic re-teaching.

sections.heading: What IGCSE maths tutoring costs around Al Barsha South, and what the premium buys
paragraphs: Parents in this cluster usually want the number before anything else, so here it is with its sources attached. Published market rates for Dubai tutoring run from the low end upwards: EdFlik advertises from AED 45 to 65 an hour and Tutopiya from AED 33 to 52 for online sessions at the budget end, generally university-student tutors. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 an hour and IB from AED 200. TutorChase quotes AED 270. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 rate table puts in-home one-to-one visits at AED 180 to 350, with home tutors reaching AED 500, and IB, IGCSE and A Level specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above. At the top, BartyED publishes AED 650 for a premium named or examiner-led tutor. These are other providers' figures, published by them, not IB Gram's price list.

Read those bands as a market and the shape is clear: the step from AED 50 to AED 150 buys subject qualification, and the step from AED 150 to AED 300 buys syllabus specificity, which for IGCSE mathematics means a tutor who knows 0580 Extended Paper 2 as a document rather than as a topic list. The step from AED 300 to AED 650 buys scarcity, and whether it buys anything else depends entirely on the individual. The travel element is separate from all of it: Bestimate's in-home band sits above its online band for the same tutor quality, and that difference is the car, not the teaching.

Monthly figures are easier to budget against than hourly ones. Packages visible in this market include AED 799 a month for eight online sessions and AED 1,599 to 1,799 a month for four two-hour in-home sessions. Bestimate's monthly estimates for a weekly one-hour session run AED 240 to 600 at the budget end, AED 600 to 1,200 mid-market, and AED 1,000 to 2,000 and above for specialist exam-year support. Set against Dubai school fees, which KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 would not rise for the 2026-27 academic year, a weekly specialist session is a visible but not unusual addition to an exam-year budget. IB Gram does not publish a rate card on this page; the free trial lesson and the consultation exist so a family sees the tutor before discussing money.

sections.heading: Online or in-home for an Al Barsha South maths student
paragraphs: IB Gram does not offer home visits in the UAE. Tutoring for UAE families is delivered one-to-one over live video, and in-home visiting is a service offered only in India. That is worth saying plainly on a page a parent reached by searching for a tutor, because the honest version of the comparison favours video for this subject in this location anyway.

The in-home argument is real and it is about attention. A tutor in the room can see a student's page, catch a dropped minus sign as it happens, and stop a phone being picked up. Those are genuine advantages and anyone who pretends otherwise is selling. What they cost is tutor choice and time. A visiting tutor has to live within a sensible drive of Al Barsha South and be free in the narrow window between the school run and dinner, which for a specialist in 0580 Extended non-calculator technique may mean nobody is available at all. The travel premium in the published Dubai bands is AED 30 to 150 an hour depending on tier, and the journey itself consumes the slot either side of the lesson.

Video removes the geography and keeps most of the attention, provided the setup is right. A shared digital whiteboard where the student writes and the tutor annotates reproduces the dropped-minus-sign catch almost exactly, and the session recording lets the student rewatch the working, which no in-home lesson provides. For a mathematics subject specifically, the screen is a closer substitute than it is for a conversational subject, because the work is written and both parties are looking at the same written page. The trade-off a family should weigh is honest: in-home buys physical presence at a travel premium from a smaller pool; online buys the specialist and the recording, and requires the student to sit at a desk with the door open.

sections.heading: The exam calendar counted backwards from a UAE candidate's series
paragraphs: Cambridge International runs IGCSE, O Level and International A Level examinations in a June series and a November series. UAE candidates sit those two. The February and March series exists but is offered to India only, so any revision plan built around a spring exam window is built for the wrong country, and a parent in Al Barsha South should treat a tutor who suggests one as not knowing the market. Cambridge also allocates every examination centre to one of six administrative zones, and states that it is essential to use the correct version of the timetable for the centre's zone, adding that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an examination after using the wrong zone timetable. That is the school's job, but it is worth a parent asking which zone their child's centre sits in.

Pearson Edexcel International GCSE examinations run in May/June and November each year. For the November 2026 series the final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026, with results reaching students in January; November 2025 results landed with students on 22 January 2026. June 2026 results went to centres on 19 August 2026 and to students on 20 August 2026. Pearson publishes provisional timetables well ahead of each series, which is why every date above should be confirmed against the live official timetable rather than trusted from a tutoring page, including this one.

Counting backwards is where the plan comes from. If the target is a June series, the school's entry decisions and tier choices are usually locked by the preceding term, mock examinations land in the winter, and the last useful window for genuinely learning new content closes about ten weeks before the first paper. Everything after that point is technique, timing and past papers, because a topic learned three weeks before a paper is not reliable under pressure. A family starting in September has two content terms and a technique term. A family starting in March for a June series has a technique term only, and the honest plan says so and prioritises the topics with the highest mark yield rather than the ones the student dislikes least.

sections.heading: KHDA, the inspection report, and what it tells you about your child's maths teaching
paragraphs: Dubai's private schools are regulated by the Knowledge and Human Development Authority, which u.ae describes as responsible for enhancing and overseeing the quality of private education in the emirate. KHDA inspects annually and publishes a report per school on a six-band scale from Outstanding down to Very Weak. For a parent in Al Barsha South trying to work out whether a maths problem is their child's or their school's, the published report is the only independent evidence available, and it is free to read on the regulator's own site.

What to look for is narrower than the headline band. The report breaks attainment and progress down by subject and by phase, so a school rated Good overall can be rated Acceptable for secondary mathematics attainment, and that distinction is the one that matters to a Year 11 family. The report also comments on the quality of teaching and on assessment, and an inspection note that a school's assessment data does not match external outcomes is a direct explanation for a predicted 7 arriving as a 5. None of this means the school is failing the student. It means the family knows which gap they are paying a tutor to cover.

The surrounding context is worth having too. Dubai had 387,441 private-school students across 227 private schools in 2024-25, offering 17 different curricula, with the UK curriculum on 37% of enrolment, Indian on 26%, US on 14% and International Baccalaureate on 7%. Seven new private schools open for the 2026-27 intake, four UK curriculum and three IB, creating 16,846 new places, after six opened during 2025-26 and enrolment rose 6%. KHDA confirmed on 22 May 2026 that there would be no increase in private school fees for 2026-27 under Dubai's second economic incentives package. A market expanding that fast has uneven staffing, and subject-level variation between two schools a kilometre apart in Al Barsha South is the normal consequence.

sections.heading: Is your tutor legally permitted to teach in the UAE, and how a parent checks
paragraphs: Private tutoring in the UAE is regulated by permit. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023 Regarding the Introduction of Private Tuition Work Permits. The permit is granted free of charge for two years, and eligible applicants include teachers registered in government or private schools, employees in the government and private sectors, unemployed individuals, school students aged 15 to 18, and university students. MoHRE's own service page for it is titled Issuance of a New Work Permit - Private Tutor Licensing, lists no fees and a two-working-day completion time, and is applied for through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system.

Two consequences follow for a family in Al Barsha South. The first is that anyone offering private lessons in the UAE without that permit is operating outside the rules: u.ae states that individuals offering private tutoring without a permit from MoHRE will be subject to fines and penalties outlined in the applicable laws. No fine schedule is published, so no amount should be quoted to you, and a page that quotes one is guessing. The second is that the permit is free and takes two working days, which removes the usual excuse. A tutor who says the paperwork is expensive or slow has not applied.

The other rule worth knowing concerns your child's own teachers. In Abu Dhabi, ADEK's professional-ethics rules for private and charter school staff prohibit teachers from providing paid private tutoring to students enrolled at their own school, and the MoHRE permit's code of conduct also bars serving students affiliated with the permit holder's own school. Those are press-reported positions and worth verifying against the current policy document, but the direction is unambiguous: your child's own maths teacher is not the right person to hire privately, however convenient it looks. A tutoring operation with premises and staff in Dubai is a different legal animal again and needs a KHDA Educational Services Permit for a training institute. IB Gram holds no KHDA permit, operates no UAE centre, and is not approved, accredited or licensed by KHDA, ADEK, SPEA, MoE, MoHRE, Cambridge, Pearson or the IB.

sections.heading: Academic honesty: what a maths tutor may and may not do with your child's work
paragraphs: IGCSE mathematics has no coursework component at either board for the main mathematics syllabuses, which removes most of the honesty risk that shadows IB and A Level tutoring. The boundary still matters, because students in this cluster often take other subjects that do carry assessed work, and because 0607 includes an investigation paper where the line is live. The rule is simple and we apply it everywhere: a tutor teaches, explains, reviews and gives feedback on work the student has produced. A tutor does not produce the work.

In practice that means a tutor may work through a past-paper question with a student, mark the student's attempt, explain why the mark scheme awarded what it did, set similar questions, and show a model method on a different question. A tutor may not sit beside a student during a timed school assessment, supply answers to a piece of work that will be submitted for assessment, write or part-write an Internal Assessment or an investigation, or edit a student's coursework into a submittable state. Providers exist in this market that sell completed Internal Assessments. That is an academic-integrity breach, it triggers malpractice procedures against the student rather than the seller, and it is not a service IB Gram offers at any price.

There is a second boundary around materials. We reference IB, Cambridge and Pearson syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes and grade-boundary tables and link to the official source, and we do not reproduce or supply them as downloads. For a maths family the practical version of this is reassuring rather than restrictive: everything a student needs for 0580 or 4MA1 preparation is published by the board, free, on the board's own site, and a good tutor's value is in knowing which question to give next and how to mark it, not in holding a private library.

sections.heading: MoE equivalency: what an IGCSE maths grade has to do with UAE university entry
paragraphs: Families in Al Barsha South planning to keep their child in the UAE for university eventually meet the Ministry of Education equivalency process, and mathematics sits inside it. For the British track, students must submit proof of one accredited subject at Advanced Level with a grade of no less than E, or two accredited subjects at Advanced Subsidiary Level with the same grade, and must pass five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates with a grade of no less than E or grade 3. Arabic and Islamic education are not included among the five required subjects.

That five-subject rule is worth stating precisely, because at least one ranking competitor page tells UAE parents that six IGCSE subjects are required. The sourced figure is five, excluding Arabic and Islamic Education. The grade floor is low - E or grade 3 - which surprises parents who assume equivalency demands strong grades. It does not. What demands strong grades is the university course, and mathematics is where that bites: a quantitative degree will set its own entry requirement well above an equivalency floor.

For the American track, English proficiency requires a score of 5 in the IELTS academic test, 61 in the TOEFL iBT test, or 450 in the reading and writing section of the SAT, and mathematics requires at least 450 in the SAT Math test before applying. No IB points threshold appears in the sourced article, so no IB equivalency figure should be published without a moe.gov.ae source, and this page does not publish one. Equivalency is a process the Ministry runs, not something a tutoring service performs, guarantees or accelerates. Check the current requirements on the Ministry's own channel, and treat anyone who offers to secure equivalency for you with suspicion.

sections.heading: Arabic, Islamic Education and Social Studies alongside IGCSE maths
paragraphs: A detail that catches new arrivals in Al Barsha South: the mandatory UAE subjects run alongside whichever international curriculum the school is licensed for. Arabic, Islamic Education and Social and Moral Studies are mandatory in all Dubai private schools regardless of the licensed international curriculum, and KHDA's requirements must be implemented by the start of the 2025-26 academic year, or April 2026 for schools whose year starts in April. The federal baseline behind this is that private schools are not obliged to follow a specific curriculum beyond Arabic language, social studies and Islamic studies, but must adhere to the Ministry's general regulations.

The organisational rules are specific, and they explain a timetable a parent might otherwise find puzzling. For Arabic as a first language, Islamic Education and Social Studies, schools must organise separate classes for Arabs and non-Arabs, and combined classes for both groups are strictly prohibited due to the different curriculum expectations and language of instruction. KHDA requires Standard Arabic as the main language of instruction for Islamic Education for Arabs and for Arabic as a first language, Arabic as the primary language for Social Studies for Arab students, and the school's licensed-curriculum language for non-Arabs in Islamic Education and in Moral, Social and Cultural studies. Schools are required to ensure that all teachers of Islamic Education and Arabic have appropriate KHDA approval to teach these subjects.

Why this appears on a mathematics page is timetable arithmetic. KHDA calculates mandatory-subject instructional time on a 40-minute lesson unit, allows schools to vary lesson length provided total weekly time is met, and advises that any mandatory subject lesson should be at least 25 minutes. Those periods come out of the same week as IGCSE mathematics, so a Year 11 student in Dubai carries a fuller timetable than the same student would in the UK. When a family is deciding whether to add a weekly maths session, the honest question is not whether the child has an hour spare but which hour it comes from. One further constraint: for the mandatory UAE subjects, the use of any different or additional content without prior permission from the MoE is strictly prohibited, so tutoring support in those subjects stays inside the school's own material.

sections.heading: Getting started, and the honest version of what happens next
paragraphs: The first step is a free trial lesson, and the trial is a diagnostic rather than a demonstration. The tutor asks for the exam board, the syllabus code, the tier and the most recent marked assessment before the session, then works through a section of a real past paper with the student live. By the end a parent has something concrete: a list of topics by accuracy band, the four-way split of where marks were lost, and a view on whether one session a week or two is the right starting point. The trial is free with no card required; if the match is wrong, nothing continues.

Matching takes a few days rather than minutes, because the match is to a syllabus code and a specific weakness. For IGCSE mathematics the pool is deep, so a 0580 Extended or 4MA1 Higher request is usually filled quickly. The honest exception is worth stating: for an unusual combination - 0607 with the investigation paper, say, alongside a specific transition into AS Further Mathematics - the right specialist may not be free in the slot a family wants. We say so rather than placing a general maths tutor and calling it a specialist match. A family that is told the truth about availability can decide to wait a week or to shift the slot.

After the first month the plan is reviewed against evidence rather than feeling. The topic-accuracy record from the trial is re-run on a fresh paper section, and the four causes are re-counted. If the working-not-shown figure has dropped and the content gap has not, the plan shifts towards teaching. If content is closing and timing is not, the plan shifts to timed sections. Sessions pause for school exam weeks and for travel, and the slot holds. Nobody at IB Gram will promise a grade, because no tutor can deliver one. What a tutor can deliver is a student who claims the method marks that are already on the page in front of them.

faqs.question: Which IGCSE maths syllabus does my child in Al Barsha South actually sit?
faqs.answer: Check the school's exam entry confirmation, not the textbook. Three codes dominate this cluster: Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics 0580, Cambridge International Mathematics 0607, and Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A 4MA1. The code decides the paper structure and the practice material. A 0580 Extended candidate sits a non-calculator Paper 2 and a calculator Paper 4; a 4MA1 Higher candidate may use a calculator on both papers; a 0607 candidate is expected to work with a graphics display calculator and faces an investigation-style paper. Practising the wrong board's papers feels productive and targets the wrong assessment, so send us the code before the trial lesson.

faqs.question: Is Core or Extended the right entry for my child, and can it still be changed?
faqs.answer: A Cambridge 0580 Core entry is capped at grade C and an Extended entry runs A* to E, so the tier choice can close a door before the exam is sat. If your child wants A Level Mathematics or IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches, a capped entry is a problem. The reverse error is real too: an Extended entry for a student scoring consistently below 40% on past papers can yield a lower grade than Core would, because Extended offers fewer accessible marks. Entry decisions sit with the school and are usually reviewable within the board's deadline. Bring a marked paper at both tiers to that conversation.

faqs.question: Why did my child's mock come back as a 5 when the school predicted a 7?
faqs.answer: Usually because the prediction was based on topic tests and the mock was a full timed paper, which tests different things. Four causes account for most of the gap: topics never properly learned, arithmetic slips on method the student knew, questions started and abandoned on time, and correct answers written with no working, which forfeits the method marks. Only the first needs more teaching. The others are habit, fluency and timing problems that respond to a few weeks of targeted correction. Mark the paper, classify every lost mark by cause, and the remedy becomes obvious instead of general.

faqs.question: How do method marks work in an IGCSE maths mark scheme?
faqs.answer: Mark schemes allocate M marks for a correct method and A marks for accuracy. A student who does three steps mentally and writes one number receives the accuracy mark if the number is right and nothing at all if it is wrong. Over a full Paper 4 that habit typically costs ten to fifteen marks, which on most series is a whole grade. Fixing it requires no new mathematics: the student writes every intermediate line, and the tutor marks their own script against the official mark scheme aloud so the student hears which lines earned marks. Three weeks of consistent correction usually embeds it.

faqs.question: My child is fine with a calculator and falls apart without one. What is going on?
faqs.answer: That is a mechanical fluency problem, not a conceptual one, and it is very common among students taught largely on a calculator. Cambridge 0580 Paper 2 at Extended is non-calculator, so fractions, negatives, indices, surds and standard form all have to be manipulated by hand at speed. The fix is short daily drill on exactly those operations rather than re-teaching topics the student already understands. Expect three to six weeks for the slips to drop meaningfully. It is worth fixing properly at 16, because IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches and A Level Pure both assume that fluency as automatic.

faqs.question: How much do IGCSE maths tutors charge around Al Barsha South?
faqs.answer: Published Dubai market rates spread widely. At the budget end, Tutopiya advertises from AED 33 to 52 an hour and EdFlik from AED 45 to 65, usually university-student tutors. Unitors publishes IGCSE tuition from AED 150 an hour. TutorChase quotes AED 270. Bestimate's Tutoring Cost Dubai 2026 table puts in-home one-to-one at AED 180 to 350 and specialists at AED 200 to 450 and above, while BartyED publishes AED 650 for premium examiner-led work. Those are each provider's own published figures, not IB Gram's prices. We run a free trial lesson first and discuss cost after you have seen the tutor teach.

faqs.question: Does IB Gram send a tutor to our villa in Al Barsha South?
faqs.answer: No. IB Gram does not offer home visits anywhere in the UAE; visiting tutors are a service we run only in India. UAE lessons are delivered one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time. For mathematics specifically the substitution is close, because a shared digital whiteboard lets the tutor annotate the student's working line by line, which is most of what an in-room tutor does. It also removes the travel premium visible in published Dubai rates and widens the pool from tutors who live nearby to specialists in the exact paper your child sits.

faqs.question: When are the IGCSE exams for a UAE candidate, and is there a spring series?
faqs.answer: Cambridge International runs IGCSE examinations in a June series and a November series, and UAE candidates sit those. The February and March series is offered to India only, so a revision plan built around a spring window is built for the wrong country. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May/June and November; the November 2026 final timetable runs from late October to 19 November 2026. Cambridge allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and warns that the correct zone timetable must be used. Always confirm dates against the board's live official timetable, which can be revised.

faqs.question: Which topics lose the most marks on 0580 Extended Paper 4?
faqs.answer: In the scripts we mark, four areas recur. Frequency density for histograms with unequal class widths is mishandled more often than any other single calculation. The length, area and volume scale-factor relationship for similar solids is answered wrongly most series. Without-replacement tree diagrams fail structurally, because the second-branch probabilities are not adjusted and every later mark falls with them. Reverse percentages invite division where multiplication is needed, with no method mark for a plausible wrong route. None of these are conceptually hard. All four are reliably worth marks once the student has met them under timed conditions.

faqs.question: We are six weeks from the papers. Is it too late to start tutoring?
faqs.answer: Not too late to be useful, but the plan has to change shape. Six weeks is a technique window, not a content window: a topic learned three weeks before a paper is not reliable under pressure. So the work becomes timed sections, mark-scheme marking, claiming method marks, and targeting the two or three highest-yield topics the student can still move. We would mark a full paper in the first session and be explicit about what is reachable and what is not. A tutor who promises to cover the whole syllabus in six weeks is selling something they cannot deliver.

faqs.question: Is the maths tutor we hire in Al Barsha South legally permitted to teach here?
faqs.answer: They should be. The MoHRE private tutor work permit was introduced by Ministerial Resolution No. 710 of 2023, is granted free of charge for two years, and is issued through the MoHRE smart app, website and e-services system with a stated two-working-day completion time. Eligible applicants include registered school teachers, government and private sector employees, unemployed residents, university students, and school students aged 15 to 18. Individuals tutoring without a permit are subject to fines and penalties under the applicable laws, though no fine schedule is published. Ask to see the permit itself. Since it is free and quick, there is no credible reason not to hold one.

faqs.question: Can a tutor help with my child's maths coursework or investigation?
faqs.answer: A tutor teaches, explains, marks and gives feedback on work the student has produced. A tutor does not write, part-write or edit an assessed task into a submittable state. The main Cambridge and Pearson IGCSE mathematics syllabuses carry no coursework, so this mostly arises with 0607's investigation paper and with other subjects. On those we coach method and process, review the student's own draft, and set comparable practice on different material. Providers in this market sell completed Internal Assessments; that is an integrity breach which puts the student at risk of malpractice proceedings, and it is not something IB Gram offers.

faqs.question: Does a strong IGCSE maths grade matter for Ministry of Education equivalency?
faqs.answer: Less than parents expect. For the British track the Ministry of Education requires five accredited subjects in GCSE or IGCSE certificates at a grade of no less than E or grade 3, plus one accredited subject at Advanced Level at no less than E or two at Advanced Subsidiary Level at the same grade. Arabic and Islamic education are not counted among the five. One competitor page currently tells UAE parents six subjects are needed, which is wrong. The grade floor is low, so equivalency is rarely the binding constraint; the university course's own entry requirement usually is. Verify current rules on the Ministry's own channel.

faqs.question: What time can an online maths session realistically start on a school day?
faqs.answer: For most Al Barsha South families, 4.30pm is the earliest workable start and 5pm is more common. School buses serving Al Barsha South 4 and 5, Arjan and the Jumeirah Village communities often deliver students home after 4pm, and a student who walks in at 4.10pm is not ready to sit a timed section at 4.15pm. Families working in Dubai Internet City and Media City frequently prefer 6.30pm or 7pm so a parent is home. Because the lesson is online, the slot is not shortened by a tutor's drive across Al Khail Road at either end.

faqs.question: How do I know whether the problem is my child or the school's maths teaching?
faqs.answer: Read the school's KHDA inspection report, which is published on the regulator's own site and broken down by subject and phase. A school rated Good overall can be rated Acceptable for secondary mathematics attainment, and that is the line a Year 11 family needs. The report also comments on assessment quality, and a note that internal data does not match external outcomes directly explains a predicted 7 arriving as a 5. Dubai had 227 private schools and 387,441 private-school students in 2024-25, with seven more schools opening for 2026-27, so subject-level variation between neighbouring schools is normal.

faqs.question: What happens if no specialist is free for my child's exact combination?
faqs.answer: We tell you. For mainstream requests - 0580 Extended, 4MA1 Higher - the pool is deep and matching usually takes a few days. For an unusual combination, such as 0607 with its investigation paper alongside a transition into AS Further Mathematics, the right specialist may not be available in the slot you want. The honest options are to wait, to move the slot, or to start with a strong generalist on a clearly stated interim basis. What we will not do is place a general maths tutor and describe them as a syllabus specialist, which is the standard practice this page exists to avoid.

intro.heading: The maths homework cycle, and the hour it actually leaves you
paragraphs: Mathematics is the subject where the Al Furjan afternoon bites hardest, because maths homework is usually set to be done the same evening and marked the next day. The bus reaches the Quortaj district around 15:25 and the Murooj district closer to 15:50; a Year 11 student who stayed for a revision clinic is home at 16:30. By the time a snack and a change of clothes have happened, the window for serious algebra is the 17:00 to 19:30 band and nothing earlier.

That matters because maths tutoring works differently from most subjects. It is cumulative, so a session that lands in the same week as the topic being taught is worth several sessions landing a month later. A weekly slot that actually holds through fixtures, clinics and traffic is therefore more valuable in mathematics than in any other subject on the timetable, and the slot that holds is almost never the earliest one.

The second constraint is the paper. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics is syllabus 0580 and the Pearson Edexcel International GCSE equivalent is 4MA1. They set different numbers of papers, name their tiers differently, provide different formula support and mark to different conventions. A tutor working from the wrong board's past papers teaches good lessons at the wrong target, and in a terminal-exam subject nobody finds out until the mock.

IB Gram matches on the code and tier from the school's own entry list, and delivers every UAE lesson one-to-one over live video on Gulf Standard Time between 15:30 and 21:30. No tutor attends a UAE address, since home visiting is a service we run only in India. In Al Furjan that removes the constraint that keeps the local pool small: nobody is driving into the villa districts, so the tutor is chosen on the paper rather than on the postcode.

The rest of this page is practical. It sets out the paper structure for both boards, where marks go topic by topic rather than which topics feel hard, how the tier decision should be made from marked evidence, why the calculator and non-calculator papers need separate work, and a term-by-term plan for Year 10 that fits around this community's afternoons.

One scheduling note worth having before you read on. UAE candidates sit the June series and the November series; Cambridge's February and March series is offered to India only. In the four weeks of study leave before the June series the whole afternoon frees up, and that fortnight is the most contested period in the Dubai tutoring year, so it is worth booking well in advance. The other date worth knowing is the entry deadline, which falls months before the papers and fixes the tier your child will sit. Once it passes, the only remaining variable is performance on a paper already chosen, which is why the useful conversations about tier belong in Year 10 rather than the spring of Year 11.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-furjan.programmesIntro: Mathematics support in this corridor divides into four stages, and the handover between them is where most grades are lost. These are the stages and what each one actually needs.

programmes.name: Key Stage 3 mathematics, Years 7 to 9
programmes.description: The three years that decide whether Extended tier is viable. Four skills matter: fluent arithmetic without a calculator, rearranging a formula without guessing, confident work with negatives and fractions in algebra, and showing method as a habit. None is assessed externally, so a gap persists invisibly until Year 10 brings questions that require all four at once.
programmes.countryNote: Year 7 to 9 students in Al Furjan are home earlier than exam-year students, often by 16:00, so a 16:30 session fits comfortably and leaves the evening clear. This is the cheapest stage to buy support and the one families skip. A single weekly session through Year 9 costs less than a Year 11 intensive block and changes which tier is open to the student.

programmes.name: IGCSE Mathematics, Years 10 to 11
programmes.description: Two years ending in terminal written papers, with the tier fixed at entry. Cambridge 0580 runs Core and Extended; Pearson 4MA1 runs Foundation and Higher. Most lost marks are method marks rather than knowledge: a student who produces a correct answer from a calculator without writing the steps forfeits marks they earned. Topic revision does not fix that.
programmes.countryNote: This is where most Al Furjan enquiries sit. Year 10 students are home between 15:40 and 16:10 on local routes; Year 11 students with revision clinics are later. A 17:00 or 17:30 start is the usual fit, moving to two shorter sessions a week from the mock window. Study leave before the June series frees the afternoon entirely for paper work.

programmes.name: Additional and Further Pure Mathematics
programmes.description: Cambridge 0606 and Pearson 4PM1, sat alongside the main mathematics entry by students heading for Advanced Level mathematics or IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches Higher Level. Calculus, logarithms and trigonometric identities arrive a year early, which makes the post-16 transition far less abrupt. It is examined in its own right, not as enrichment.
programmes.countryNote: This is the most under-taught subject in the Al Furjan corridor and the hardest to match locally, because few tutors have taught it recently. Students who take it arrive at Advanced Level or Diploma mathematics with the first term's content already familiar, which is worth more than any amount of summer revision. Where a school does not offer it, the content can still be used as a bridging syllabus.

programmes.name: Advanced Level or IB Diploma mathematics
programmes.description: Both routes normally require grade 6 or 7 at IGCSE, and both move considerably faster than Year 11. Advanced Level mathematics expects algebraic fluency from week one; IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches expects the same plus early proof. Students entered for Core or Foundation tier frequently find both closed, which is the real cost of a tier decision.
programmes.countryNote: Al Furjan families moving into the IB Diploma generally change schools, since full Diploma provision in the Jebel Ali corridor is thinner than further north. The bridging block between Extended IGCSE and Diploma mathematics is four to six summer sessions and is the best-value purchase in the whole sequence, because the alternative is catching up while also settling into a new school.

dubai/igcse-maths-tutor-in-al-furjan.subjectsIntro: IGCSE mathematics is one qualification but a dozen separate skills, and marks cluster in predictable places. These are the areas an Al Furjan family will hear about most, with what each one costs when it is weak.

subjects.name: Number and accuracy
subjects.description: Standard form, bounds, ratio, percentage change and reverse percentages. Upper and lower bounds are the reliable loss here: students treat them as a topic to memorise rather than a rule about measurement, and lose whole questions on rounding and accuracy demands they did not read.

subjects.name: Algebraic manipulation
subjects.description: Expanding, factorising, rearranging and solving. The commonest cause of lost marks across the whole paper, because almost every other topic routes through it. Negatives and fractions in the same expression are where fluency breaks, and that is a drill problem rather than a teaching problem.

subjects.name: Equations and inequalities
subjects.description: Linear, simultaneous and quadratic equations, including the formula and completing the square at Extended tier. Students lose marks by abandoning method once the calculator gives a root, which forfeits the working marks that make up most of the question's value.

subjects.name: Coordinate geometry and graphs
subjects.description: Gradients, midpoints, parallel and perpendicular lines, and sketching curves. Reading a gradient from two plotted points instead of from the line of best fit is a mark-scheme error that appears in both mathematics and science papers, and one session fixes it for good.

subjects.name: Functions and transformations
subjects.description: Function notation, composite and inverse functions, and transformations of graphs. Notation is the barrier rather than concept: students who decode function notation each time it appears run out of time, while students who read it fluently answer in half the time.

subjects.name: Geometry and angle reasoning
subjects.description: Circle theorems, polygon angles, congruence and similarity. Marks here go to the reason as much as the answer, and an unstated theorem is a lost mark even with the correct angle. Writing the reason is a habit worth drilling early.

subjects.name: Mensuration
subjects.description: Area, volume, surface area, arcs and sectors. Routine when practised and expensive when not, because the questions are usually multi-step and compound shapes require a plan before any calculation. Students who start calculating before decomposing the shape lose time and accuracy.

subjects.name: Trigonometry
subjects.description: Right-angled trigonometry, the sine and cosine rules, bearings and three-dimensional problems. Bearings questions lose marks for the diagram rather than the calculation, and three-dimensional questions lose them for not identifying the relevant triangle before starting.

subjects.name: Vectors and transformations
subjects.description: Column vectors, magnitude, and geometric proof using vectors. Short questions with high mark density, frequently skipped in revision because they look unfamiliar. A handful of sessions makes them reliable, which is a good return on time this late in the course.

subjects.name: Probability
subjects.description: Tree diagrams, conditional probability and set notation. The structure of the tree does most of the work, so students who draw it carefully rarely lose marks, and students who attempt it mentally rarely keep them. Set notation is examined and often untaught.

subjects.name: Statistics and data handling
subjects.description: Cumulative frequency, histograms with unequal intervals, box plots and averages from grouped data. Histograms with unequal class widths are the single most reliably lost topic in the data section, because frequency density is skipped in class as often as it is examined.

subjects.name: Additional Mathematics
subjects.description: Calculus, logarithms, series and trigonometric identities, sat alongside the main entry. The best available bridge into Advanced Level or IB Diploma mathematics, and the hardest subject in this list to find a locally based tutor for in the Al Furjan corridor.

sections.heading: Which maths paper your child actually sits
paragraphs: Before anything else, establish the code. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics is 0580, with Core and Extended tiers. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A is 4MA1, with Foundation and Higher tiers. Schools in the Al Furjan corridor use both, and more than one enters a different board for mathematics than for the sciences, so the assumption that a school has one board is unsafe. The exams officer holds the entry list that settles it.

The practical differences are not cosmetic. The number of papers differs, the calculator provision across papers differs, the formula support given in the exam room differs, and the mark-scheme conventions differ in how method is credited. Past papers from the wrong board look close enough to be plausible and are different enough to misdirect a term of revision. This is the quietest way to waste tutoring money in Dubai.

Tier names cause their own confusion. A parent told their child is on Higher tier may assume that is the top of the range; in Cambridge terms the equivalent is Extended. Conversely Foundation and Core sound milder than they are: both cap the grade available, and the cap is the thing that matters for post-16 entry. Ask which tier, which board, and what grade the tier reaches.

A tutor who knows the paper will state its structure without checking. That is the single best five-second test available to a parent, and it works because structure is what planning depends on. A revision plan that treats every component equally was written by somebody who did not know which component your child is losing marks on, and that is most generic plans.

sections.heading: Where the marks actually go, topic by topic
paragraphs: Ask which topics are hardest and every answer is the same. Ask where marks are lost and the pattern is specific, consistent across cohorts, and mostly fixable. Method not shown is the largest category by a distance: in multi-step questions the working earns marks independently of the answer, so a student who takes a result from the calculator and writes only the number forfeits marks they genuinely earned.

The second category is reading. Bounds and accuracy questions are lost because the demand about rounding was not read. Bearings questions are lost on the diagram rather than the trigonometry. Histogram questions are lost because unequal class widths were not noticed and frequency density was never used. In each case the mathematics was available to the student and the instruction was not followed.

The third is unstated reasoning in geometry. Circle theorem questions award marks for naming the theorem as well as for the angle, and students who write the number alone lose half the available credit. This is a habit rather than a concept, which makes it quick to fix and easy to overlook in a plan built around topics the student finds difficult.

The fourth is the skipped topic. Vectors and set notation are short, mark-dense and frequently left out of revision because they look unfamiliar. For a student in the final term, they are usually the fastest marks available on the whole paper. A tutor working from the marked mock, rather than from a syllabus checklist, finds those before anything else.

sections.heading: The tier decision, made from marked evidence rather than hope
paragraphs: Entry tier caps the grade, and in mathematics it is the decision with the longest shadow. Cambridge Core and Pearson Foundation entries cannot reach the top grades, and most British-curriculum schools want grade 6 or 7 before accepting a subject at Advanced Level, with IB Diploma Higher Level entry usually asking the same. So a tier chosen in Year 10 can close a post-16 route in a subject the student is capable of.

Schools generally recommend on the evidence of Year 10 performance, and they are usually right. Where parents can add value is in understanding what the evidence says rather than arguing with the conclusion. Three marked papers answer the question. If the losses are content, the gap is closable in a term. If they are method and reading, the student is stronger than the mark suggests. If algebraic fluency itself is absent, the lower tier is the honest answer.

The uncomfortable half of this is real. A student pushed into Extended or Higher tier on ambition can score below what they would have achieved on the lower paper, because the questions assume fluency they do not have and the time pressure compounds it. A grade kept at the lower tier is worth more than a grade lost at the higher one, and no tutor should pretend otherwise to keep a booking.

The timing is the point of this section. All of this is a Year 10 conversation. By the spring of Year 11 the entry window has closed and the only remaining variable is how well the student performs on the paper they are already entered for. Families in this corridor who book a weekly session in Year 10 get that conversation at a useful moment; families who book in Year 11 get it as information.

sections.heading: Fitting maths into the Al Furjan afternoon
paragraphs: Mathematics homework in most Dubai schools is set for the same evening, which makes the tutoring slot a scheduling problem rather than a preference. The bus loops across Al Furjan's districts spread arrival from 15:20 to 16:10 for the same school, and Year 11 students staying for subject clinics are home around 16:30. The practical window for an hour of algebra, after food and a change of clothes, starts at 17:00 for most of this community.

Different routes give different answers, and it is worth knowing which one applies to your household. A child at a Dubai Investments Park or Green Community school can be ready at 15:50. A student travelling the Al Barsha or Al Khail corridor will not be ready before 17:00, and with a fixture it is 18:00. Booking the time that works on a good day is how families lose two sessions a month without noticing.

This is also where online delivery stops being a trade-off. A 19:15 session is impossible for a visiting tutor crossing Dubai in evening traffic and entirely routine over video. More usefully, a session missed because of a late bus moves to the next evening rather than the next week, which across a term is the difference between thirty-two sessions and twenty-four. In a cumulative subject that gap compounds.

One last pattern specific to mathematics. Where a household has two children needing maths, running consecutive slots with different tutors works better than one shared session, because a Year 8 student and a Year 11 student are working on different things at different speeds. The evening is interrupted once instead of twice, and each child gets their own written note.

sections.heading: Two papers, two different skills
paragraphs: Where an entry includes a paper sat without a calculator, that paper examines a different skill from the rest of the qualification, and it needs its own preparation. Manual arithmetic, fraction work, surd handling and algebraic manipulation done on paper are all things a student loses quietly over two years of calculator-assisted homework. The loss is invisible until a paper takes the calculator away.

The remedy is maintenance rather than revision. Ten minutes of non-calculator work in every weekly session across two years keeps the fluency alive at almost no cost. Attempting to rebuild it in the final six weeks is possible and expensive, because fluency responds to frequency and there is no frequency left by then. This is the main argument for starting mathematics support in Year 10 rather than Year 11.

The calculator paper has its own discipline. Marks are available for working even when technology produced the answer, so the habit to teach is writing down what was entered and what came back. Students who present a bare number have shown no method, and in multi-step questions that is where most of the value sits. Memorising the specific model's menus also saves real time under pressure.

A practical note for this corridor: find out which calculator model the school requires and work on that one. Models differ in their statistical and table functions, and a student practising on a different model is slower and more likely to misread an output. This is a five-minute question at the start of an arrangement that saves marks in the exam room.

sections.heading: A term-by-term plan for Year 10 in this community
paragraphs: Year 10 is where mathematics grades are decided and where almost nobody plans. The shape that works in the Al Furjan corridor is simple and fits the afternoon: one weekly session from the autumn term, placed late enough to survive the bus, working on the topic being taught that week with ten minutes of non-calculator maintenance in every session. Nothing clever, and it outperforms any intensive block bought later.

The autumn term is for diagnosis and habit. Three marked pieces of school work tell a tutor whether the losses are content, method, reading or fluency, and that determines everything afterwards. The habits to establish are showing method, stating geometric reasons, and drawing a diagram before attempting bearings or three-dimensional questions. All three are behavioural and all three pay for the rest of the course.

The spring term is for tier evidence. By then there is enough marked work to have an honest conversation about Core or Extended, Foundation or Higher, before the entry window closes. This is also the term to introduce whichever topics the school covers late and students skip: vectors, set notation, histograms with unequal intervals. They are mark-dense and quick, which makes them good spring work.

The summer term of Year 10 is for first contact with whole papers. Not revision, which comes later, but learning what a full paper feels like under timing so that Year 11 mocks are not the first attempt. Two or three timed papers across that term, marked properly, changes how a student approaches Year 11. Then the Year 11 pattern is paper work, two shorter sessions a week through mocks, and study leave intensives.

sections.heading: Additional Mathematics: the bridge most families skip
paragraphs: Cambridge 0606 and Pearson 4PM1 are sat alongside the main mathematics entry, and they are the most useful qualification in this corridor that almost nobody discusses. They bring calculus, logarithms, series and trigonometric identities a year early, which means a student arriving at Advanced Level mathematics or IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches meets the first term's content as revision rather than as new material.

The case for it is strongest exactly where Al Furjan families sit. Students here commonly change schools for post-16 study, because full IB Diploma provision in the Jebel Ali corridor is thinner than further north. Arriving at a new school, with a new teaching style, and meeting calculus for the first time in the same term is a heavy load. Additional Mathematics removes one of those three variables.

The practical obstacle is supply. It is the hardest subject on this page to match with a locally based tutor, because few people have taught it recently and the Al Furjan driving pool is small to begin with. That is precisely the case where an online match earns its keep: the constraint becomes a calendar rather than a map, and the specialism survives.

Where a school does not offer the qualification at all, the content still works as a bridging syllabus over the summer after Year 11. Four to six sessions on function notation, differentiation from first principles and logarithm rules does most of the useful work, without an exam entry attached. That is a smaller commitment than the full course and still removes the first-term shock.

sections.heading: What a maths tutor will not do
paragraphs: Mathematics has less assessed coursework than most subjects, which removes one temptation but not all of them. The boundary we state at the first session is simple: a tutor teaches method, questions a student's reasoning, demonstrates technique, marks the student's own work against the board's conventions and writes down the feedback. A tutor does not complete set work, produce answers to be submitted as the student's, or sit beside a student during an assessed task.

On materials, we do not reproduce or distribute Cambridge or Pearson syllabus documents, past papers, mark schemes or grade-boundary tables. Those are cited and linked, and sessions work from what the school has issued to the student. A tutor handing over a folder of downloaded board material is distributing something that is not theirs to give, and for unreleased material that is a malpractice exposure for the student.

We also do not guarantee grades. No provider honestly can, and a promised grade is a sales device rather than a teaching plan. What can be stated is where marks are available and how they are typically lost, which is what this page has done. A page that promises a 9 and does not mention method marks is selling confidence rather than mathematics.

Finally, tutors are not described as examiners without evidence of current status, and examiner status would not give anyone access to marking, boundaries or paper content in any case. In a market where that claim is common and rarely evidenced, declining to make it is a more useful signal than making it.

whyPoints.description: The largest category of lost marks in IGCSE mathematics is working not shown. We teach that as a habit from the first session rather than as an exam tip in the final term, because it affects every multi-step question on every paper.

whyPoints.description: Additional Mathematics in particular is hard to staff from anyone willing to drive into the villa districts for 17:00. Online matching replaces the map with a calendar, which is how a scarce specialism reaches this community at all.

whyPoints.title: Honest about tier and about limits
whyPoints.description: If marked evidence says the lower tier protects the grade, we say so even though it is the less flattering answer. If no specialist is free for your subject and slot, we say that too. No grade guarantees and no unevidenced examiner claims appear anywhere on this page.

faqs.question: Which maths syllabus does my child in Al Furjan sit, 0580 or 4MA1?
faqs.answer: Ask the school's exams officer for the entry list, which names the board, the syllabus code and the tier. Cambridge IGCSE Mathematics is 0580 with Core and Extended tiers; Pearson Edexcel International GCSE Mathematics A is 4MA1 with Foundation and Higher. Schools in this corridor use both, and more than one enters a different board for mathematics than for the sciences, so assuming one board per school is unsafe. Past papers from the wrong board look plausible and misdirect a whole term of revision.

faqs.question: What time can a maths session realistically start after the Al Furjan school bus?
faqs.answer: For most of this community, 17:00. Bus loops across the Quortaj, Masakin, Dar and Murooj districts spread arrival from 15:20 to 16:10 for the same school, and Year 11 students staying for revision clinics are home closer to 16:30. Children on Dubai Investments Park or Green Community routes can start at 15:50. Students travelling the Al Barsha corridor need 18:00, and 19:00 on a fixture day. Book the time that holds on a slow afternoon rather than a quick one.

faqs.question: Why is my child losing marks in maths when the answers look right?
faqs.answer: Almost always method not shown. In multi-step questions the working earns marks independently of the final answer, so a result taken from a calculator and written as a bare number forfeits marks the student genuinely earned. The other reliable losses are unstated geometric reasons in circle theorem questions, where the reason carries as much credit as the angle, and accuracy demands that were not read in bounds questions. All three are habits rather than knowledge gaps, which makes them fast to fix.

faqs.question: Can my child change from Core to Extended tier in Year 11?
faqs.answer: Only inside the entry window, which closes months before the papers, so this is a Year 10 conversation rather than a Year 11 one. Core and Foundation entries cap the grade available, and most British-curriculum schools want grade 6 or 7 before accepting a subject at Advanced Level, with IB Diploma Higher Level entry usually asking the same. Three marked papers will tell you whether the gap is content, method or fluency, and only the third genuinely argues for the lower tier.

faqs.question: Does the non-calculator paper really need separate preparation?
faqs.answer: Yes, because it examines a skill the rest of the course does not maintain. Two years of calculator-assisted homework quietly erodes manual arithmetic, fraction and surd work, and paper-based algebraic manipulation, and the loss is invisible until a paper removes the calculator. Ten minutes of manual work in every weekly session holds the fluency at almost no cost. Rebuilding it in the final six weeks is possible and expensive, since fluency responds to frequency and there is none left by then.

faqs.question: Which maths topics are most often skipped and then examined?
faqs.answer: Vectors, set notation and histograms with unequal class widths. All three are mark-dense, all three appear reliably, and all three get left out of revision because they look unfamiliar rather than because they are hard. Frequency density in particular is skipped in class about as often as it is examined. For a student in the final term these are usually the fastest marks available on the paper, which is why a tutor should work from the marked mock rather than a syllabus checklist.

faqs.question: Is Additional Mathematics worth taking for an Al Furjan student?
faqs.answer: If post-16 mathematics is likely, yes. Cambridge 0606 and Pearson 4PM1 bring calculus, logarithms, series and trigonometric identities a year early, so the first term of Advanced Level or IB Mathematics Analysis and Approaches arrives as revision rather than new content. That matters particularly here, because families in this corridor usually change schools for post-16 study and would otherwise meet a new school, a new teaching style and calculus in the same term. It is also the hardest subject here to staff locally.

faqs.question: How should Year 10 maths tutoring be structured through the year?
faqs.answer: One weekly session from the autumn term, placed late enough to survive the bus, working on the topic being taught that week with ten minutes of non-calculator maintenance each time. Autumn is for diagnosis and habits: showing method, stating geometric reasons, drawing a diagram before bearings questions. Spring is for tier evidence and for the mark-dense topics schools cover late. The summer term is for first contact with whole timed papers, so that Year 11 mocks are not the first attempt.

faqs.question: Can a maths tutor sit with my child during a timed school assessment?
faqs.answer: No. A tutor teaches method, questions reasoning, demonstrates technique and marks the student's own work against the board's conventions, with the feedback written down. A tutor does not complete set work, supply answers to be submitted as the student's, or support a student during an assessed task. That boundary is stated at the first session. It is also worth knowing that a tutor should not be distributing downloaded board papers and mark schemes, which are not theirs to give.

faqs.question: How many sessions a week does a Year 11 maths student usually need?
faqs.answer: One through the autumn term, two shorter ones from the mock window, and up to three during study leave. The reason to prefer two short sessions over one long one in the mock term is that work set on Monday gets checked on Thursday rather than two weeks later. Study leave frees the whole afternoon and is the right moment for whole timed papers, but it is the most contested fortnight in the Dubai tutoring year, so book it months in advance.

faqs.question: Does the calculator model my child uses make a difference?
faqs.answer: It does. Schools in Dubai require particular graphic or scientific calculator models, and the statistical and table functions differ between them in ways that cost time under exam pressure and invite misread outputs. A tutor should know the model your child's school requires and teach on that one. Equally important is the habit of recording what was entered and what came back, because on the calculator paper a bare number shows no method and most of the value in a multi-step question sits in the method.

faqs.question: When do UAE candidates actually sit IGCSE maths?
faqs.answer: In the June series and the November series. Cambridge's February and March series is offered to India only, so a plan built around a February window is built on another country's calendar. Pearson Edexcel International GCSE runs in May and June and again in November. Cambridge also allocates every centre to one of six administrative zones and states that it is essential to use the correct zone timetable, warning that it cannot accept responsibility for candidates who miss an exam after using the wrong one.

faqs.question: Can one tutor take both of my children for maths on the same evening?
faqs.answer: Consecutively, with different tutors matched to each year group, rather than together. A Year 8 student and a Year 11 student are working on different content at different speeds, and a shared session shortchanges both. Running the slots back to back means the household loses one block of the evening instead of two, and one desk and one device serve both. Each child gets their own written session note. This is the most common arrangement in Al Furjan villa households with two school-age children.

faqs.question: My child has eight weeks until the June papers. What is worth doing?
faqs.answer: Whole timed papers, marked, with the errors grouped by cause rather than by topic, plus the mark-dense topics that revision usually skips. That means vectors, set notation and histograms with unequal intervals, alongside drilling the habit of showing method. What does not work in eight weeks is a full syllabus review, because there is no time to consolidate it. A tutor who proposes one has not looked at the marked mock, which is the document that should set the plan.

faqs.question: Is online maths tuition a compromise compared with someone at the table?
faqs.answer: For mathematics it is among the easiest subjects to deliver well online, because a session needs shared written working rather than physical presence. The student writes, the tutor sees it, and both work on the same page. It also removes the travel constraint that keeps the Al Furjan in-home pool small, which matters most for the scarcer entries such as Additional Mathematics. The genuine exception is children under eight, who are easier to hold in a room than on a call.

faqs.question: Can you guarantee a grade 7 or above in IGCSE maths?
faqs.answer: No, and no provider honestly can. What can be stated is where marks are available and how they are typically lost: method not shown, accuracy demands unread, geometric reasons unstated, bearings diagrams omitted, frequency density never used, vectors and set notation skipped. Working through that list on the evidence of a marked paper is what moves a grade. A page that promises a specific grade without mentioning method marks is selling confidence rather than teaching mathematics.
